## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\mlsysstack{75}{15}{25}{30}{35}{45}{10}{15}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="pdf"}

![](images/svg/margin_stack.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Machine Learning Systems Architecture Stack"}

*Architecture stack focus for this chapter.*

:::

_How can ML systems be compared fairly when hardware, models, data, and deployment all interact?_

Every optimization claim must eventually face deployment-representative conditions, and many do not survive the encounter. Each decision targets one dimension (latency, accuracy, throughput, or energy), but an ML system is the product of all these dimensions simultaneously: a pruned model may run faster on one accelerator yet slower on another, while a larger batch size improves accelerator utilization at the cost of violating a latency service-level agreement. Similarly, an edge device may advertise peak throughput that thermal throttling sharply reduces within minutes of sustained load, and a speedup measured on a warm, idle machine with synthetic inputs can vanish or reverse once real requests, cold caches, and competing jobs share the hardware. The challenge is not whether a local metric improves but whether the combined system improves under conditions that actually matter. Benchmarking makes such comparisons systematic rather than anecdotal. It requires defining what to measure, at what granularity (a single kernel, a full model, an end-to-end pipeline), and under which conditions (batch size, input distribution, thermal state, concurrent load). Without this structure, teams compare numbers that were never measured on the same terms, and decisions that looked sound in a spreadsheet collapse under production workloads. Choosing hardware, a model, or a deployment configuration on such numbers can commit an organization to millions of dollars of infrastructure that delivers a fraction of the capacity it was bought to provide. Benchmarking validates each optimization, bringing claims into contact with evidence and quantifying the gap between promise and delivery. In D·A·M terms, benchmarking holds co-design to account by revealing whether Data, Algorithm, and Machine were matched or merely assembled.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain the benchmark–production gap and benchmarking as D·A·M validation that tests whether optimization claims hold under representative conditions
- Design a benchmark that turns an optimization claim into a test by fixing its task, data, model, metrics, harness, and run rules
- Select micro, macro, or end-to-end granularity based on the engineering decision being tested, and compare a roofline prediction with a measurement
- Compare training and inference benchmarks using standardized run rules, time to quality, throughput, and latency percentiles
- Measure energy per inference and average power with matched measurement boundaries, windows, and duty cycles
- Determine whether a measured difference exceeds noise using repeated runs, paired tests, and confidence intervals
- Evaluate model and data quality with confidence calibration, robustness, representativeness, and slice-level metrics, and diagnose benchmark–production gaps caused by drift, thermal throttling, and dynamic load

:::

## The Benchmark–Production Gap {#sec-benchmarking-machine-learning-benchmarking-framework-70b8}

A model quantized to INT8 may benchmark 2$\times$ faster on a synthetic workload and show no improvement under real traffic with variable input sizes and concurrent requests. A pruned model may hold its accuracy on the test set and fail on the edge cases the benchmark never covered. Every engineering claim about speed, size, or energy is a number measured somewhere: on a warm accelerator or a cold one, at a batch of 256 or a batch of one, on curated test images or on whatever a camera returns at night. The **benchmark–production gap**\index{Benchmark-production gap!definition} is the difference between how a machine learning system performs under the conditions a measurement fixed and how it performs under the conditions it meets in deployment. Benchmarking is the engineering discipline that measures this gap before a deployment pays for it, and that narrows it by making the measured conditions match the deployed ones.

@Sec-hardware-acceleration ended on predictions. Its roofline placed ResNet-50's layers against an accelerator's compute and bandwidth ceilings, and at INT8 the doubled ridge point moved some of those layers off the compute roof. Before it, @sec-model-compression produced an INT8 artifact a quarter of the FP32 size, and @sec-data-selection reached target accuracy on fewer examples. Each is a favorable local number, computed for one stage in isolation, and the stages interact once they run together on a real machine under real load. Benchmarking measures which of those numbers survive. It comes before serving and operations because every later decision, from how many accelerators to provision to when to roll a model back, rests on measurements made the way this chapter prescribes.

```{python}
#| echo: false

from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim import Hardware, Engine, Models
from mlsysim.core.units import TFLOP, second
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_flop_rate, fmt_percent, fmt_time, fmt_multiple, fmt_multiple_range, check
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: resnet50-h100-sustained
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RESNET-50 ON ONE H100: PEAK VS. SUSTAINED ARITHMETIC
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Definition callout immediately below (peak vs. sustained), and
# │          the predicted-vs-measured roofline notebook in the granularity
# │          section, which reuses these values.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show the gap between the H100's peak dense FP16 rate and the
# │          model arithmetic ResNet-50 training actually sustains.
# │ Show:    Peak TFLOP/s, measured images/s, FLOPs per training image,
# │          achieved TFLOP/s, and the resulting MFU.
# │ How:     Registry peak and model FLOPs; MLPerf Training per-accelerator
# │          throughput anchor; training FLOPs = 3x forward FLOPs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, Literature
from mlsysim.core.units import GFLOPs, TFLOP, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_flop_rate, fmt_flops, fmt_rate, fmt_percent

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class ResNet50H100Sustained:
    """ResNet-50 training on one H100: peak dense FP16 rate vs. sustained model arithmetic."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    # MLPerf Training v3.1 per-accelerator throughput anchor (images per second)
    measured_rate = Literature.Benchmarks.ResNet50H100TrainThroughput.value / second
    # convention: the backward pass costs about twice the forward pass
    train_to_forward = 3

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    peak = h100.compute.peak_flops
    flops_per_image = train_to_forward * resnet.inference_flops
    achieved = (measured_rate * flops_per_image).to(TFLOP / second)
    mfu = (achieved / peak).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0.08 < mfu < 0.2, f"Prose says ResNet-50 sustains about 12 percent of H100 peak, got {mfu:.3f}.")
    check(abs(flops_per_image.to(GFLOPs).magnitude - 24.6) < 0.1, f"Expected 24.6 GFLOP per training image, got {flops_per_image}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    peak_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(peak, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    measured_ips_str = fmt_rate(measured_rate.to(1 / second).magnitude, "images/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    forward_gflop_str = fmt_flops(resnet.inference_flops, unit=GFLOPs, precision=1, commas=False)
    train_gflop_str = fmt_flops(flops_per_image, unit=GFLOPs, precision=1, commas=False)
    achieved_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(achieved, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    mfu_pct_str = fmt_percent(mfu, precision=1, commas=False, style="prose")
```

::: {#dfn-benchmarking-machine-learning-benchmarking .callout-definition title="Machine learning benchmarking"}

***Machine learning benchmarking***\index{Benchmarking!definition} is the empirical measurement of ML workloads under specified conditions, used to test claims about components, models, or end-to-end systems against representative evidence rather than peak specifications alone.

1.  **Significance**: The gap between peak and sustained performance can be large. An H100 delivers `{python} ResNet50H100Sustained.peak_tflop_per_s_str` of dense FP16 arithmetic at peak, yet ResNet-50 training at the MLPerf per-accelerator throughput of about `{python} ResNet50H100Sustained.measured_ips_str` sustains about `{python} ResNet50H100Sustained.achieved_tflop_per_s_str` of model arithmetic. That is a model FLOPs utilization (MFU, achieved model FLOP/s divided by the hardware's peak FLOP/s) of about `{python} ResNet50H100Sustained.mfu_pct_str`. Memory-bound layers, the input pipeline, and launch and synchronization overhead account for the difference. Benchmarking quantifies the actual $\EfficiencyHw$ gap for a workload; vendor spec sheets do not.
2.  **Distinction**: ML benchmarking spans multiple scopes. Micro-benchmarks isolate operations such as matrix multiplication, model-level benchmarks evaluate complete training or inference workloads, and end-to-end benchmarks include surrounding work such as data loading, preprocessing, optimization, checkpoint I/O, or serving infrastructure. The scope must match the engineering claim.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that benchmark numbers are stable references. Both the workload (new model architectures) and the hardware (new GPU generations) evolve, so a result that leads a benchmark under one version often becomes the baseline under a later version. Year-over-year comparisons are therefore meaningful only when the benchmark version is held constant.

:::

The iron law predicts how long a workload should take, and a benchmark measures how long it does; the difference between the two is the benchmark–production gap made quantitative. For bandwidth-bound workloads, the gap between peak and sustained performance follows from the memory wall\index{Memory wall!impact on GPU utilization}. Compute-bound workloads can approach peak, yet ResNet-50's training step shows how much of a nominally compute-bound workload still falls outside the arithmetic. Every later section that quotes a peak number is measured against this gap.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The iron law, whose utilization term $\EfficiencyHw$ benchmarks measure against peak, is established in @sec-introduction-iron-law-ml-systems-c32a.
:::

::: {#psp-benchmarking-fallacy-peak-performance .callout-perspective title="The fallacy of peak performance"}

A long-standing computer architecture quip calls peak performance "the performance the manufacturer guarantees you will not exceed." For ML systems, the gap can be wide because of the memory wall. A bandwidth-bound model leaves much of the advertised FLOP/s unreachable no matter how fast the arithmetic units run. Standardized benchmarks like MLPerf require systems to run specified models and data, revealing sustained performance at a documented operating point rather than a universal rate for every workload.

:::

ML benchmarking operates across three interdependent dimensions that map directly to the components of any deployed system. **System benchmarking**\index{Benchmarking!system, definition} measures whether the hardware delivers promised performance under realistic workloads or whether memory bandwidth saturation and software dispatch overhead erode the gains. **Model benchmarking**\index{Model benchmarking!definition} measures whether optimization techniques preserve model quality across the full input distribution, not just on curated test sets. **Data benchmarking**\index{Data benchmarking!definition} measures whether the model generalizes to real-world data with all its noise, bias, and distributional shift. Each dimension can independently reveal problems invisible to the others, and a system that passes all three provides far stronger deployment confidence than one evaluated along any single axis. The three dimensions do not receive equal space. System benchmarking carries most of the chapter, because its measurement problems (how a benchmark is built, at what granularity it measures, which standardized suite it follows, and how it measures training, inference, and power) also shape how models and data are evaluated. Model and data evaluation follow once that machinery is in place, and the summary asks whether all three survive live traffic.

::: {#psp-benchmarking-benchmarks-as-moving-targets .callout-perspective title="Benchmarks as moving targets"}

In traditional systems (for example, SPEC CPU), the benchmark is a *rigid specification*. A sorting algorithm is correct if it sorts the list. Correctness is absolute and unchanging. In ML systems, the benchmark is a *soft specification*: correctness is defined by a finite set of examples (ImageNet), and the world moves. A model that scores highly on ImageNet can still underperform on user photos taken years after the benchmark was created.

In computer architecture, engineers design for the benchmark because the benchmark represents the workload. In ML engineering, designing solely for the benchmark is overfitting. Robustness comes from acknowledging that the benchmark is only a proxy for a shifting reality.

:::

Three lighthouse workloads carry the chapter, each chosen because it sits in a home regime and arrives with claims from the preceding chapters. ResNet-50\index{ResNet-50!benchmarking lighthouse}, the book's compute-bound lighthouse, carries the measurement and training half. It is the MLPerf Training reference workload, with a published quality target (75.9 percent top-1 on ImageNet) and a published per-accelerator throughput, and its INT8 profile is the one @sec-model-compression modeled and @sec-hardware-acceleration placed on the roofline. MobileNetV2, compute-bound in its efficient regime, carries the deployment half. It runs on one edge board in a labeled composite scenario, a wildlife camera trap whose low-power host CPU and attached INT8 accelerator must classify each frame within its deadline on battery power. The measurements made on that board recur from the harness through the energy budget. Keyword spotting (KWS), the power-bound lighthouse, carries the power section, where the question is the energy a wake-word detector spends listening rather than how fast it answers. @Tbl-benchmarking-lighthouse-footprints lists each workload's operations and bytes, the quantities every later benchmark either confirms or refutes.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lighthouse-footprints
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LIGHTHOUSE FOOTPRINTS: OPERATIONS AND BYTES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-benchmarking-lighthouse-footprints immediately below.
# │
# │ Goal:    Give the chapter's three workloads equal compute and memory
# │          accounting before any benchmark is run.
# │ Show:    Parameters, forward FLOPs, FP32 and INT8 weight bytes, and the
# │          training state at 16 B/param.
# │ How:     Registry parameter and FLOP counts; byte widths from units;
# │          16 B/param mixed-precision Adam convention from model training.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_FP32, BYTES_INT8, GFLOPs, MFLOPs, MB, KB, byte, param
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_flops, fmt_memory, fmt_params, fmt_multiple

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class LighthouseFootprints:
    """Operations and bytes for ResNet-50, MobileNetV2, and the DS-CNN keyword spotter."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    mobilenet = Models.Vision.MobileNetV2
    kws = Models.Tiny.DS_CNN
    # convention: FP16 weights and gradients, FP32 master weights and two Adam moments
    training_bytes_per_param = 16 * byte / param

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet_fp32 = resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP32)
    resnet_int8 = resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    resnet_train = resnet.parameters * training_bytes_per_param
    mobilenet_fp32 = mobilenet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP32)
    mobilenet_int8 = mobilenet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    mobilenet_train = mobilenet.parameters * training_bytes_per_param
    kws_fp32 = kws.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP32)
    kws_int8 = kws.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    kws_train = kws.parameters * training_bytes_per_param

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check((resnet_fp32 / resnet_int8).to("").magnitude == 4, "INT8 weights must be a quarter of FP32.")
    check(resnet.inference_flops > 10 * mobilenet.inference_flops, "ResNet-50 should cost over 10x MobileNetV2 per image.")
    check(kws_int8.to(KB).magnitude < 300, "The INT8 keyword spotter should fit in a few hundred kilobytes.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet_params_str = fmt_params(resnet.parameters, scale="M", precision=1, commas=False)
    resnet_gflop_str = fmt_flops(resnet.inference_flops, unit=GFLOPs, precision=1, commas=False)
    resnet_fp32_str = fmt_memory(resnet_fp32, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    resnet_int8_str = fmt_memory(resnet_int8, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    resnet_train_str = fmt_memory(resnet_train, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    mobilenet_params_str = fmt_params(mobilenet.parameters, scale="M", precision=1, commas=False)
    mobilenet_mflop_str = fmt_flops(mobilenet.inference_flops, unit=MFLOPs, precision=0, commas=False)
    mobilenet_fp32_str = fmt_memory(round(mobilenet_fp32.to(MB).magnitude) * MB, unit=MB, precision=0, commas=False)
    mobilenet_int8_str = fmt_memory(round(mobilenet_int8.to(MB).magnitude, 1) * MB, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    mobilenet_train_str = fmt_memory(round(mobilenet_train.to(MB).magnitude, 1) * MB, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    kws_params_str = fmt_params(kws.parameters, scale="K", precision=0, commas=False)
    kws_mflop_str = fmt_flops(kws.inference_flops, unit=MFLOPs, precision=0, commas=False)
    kws_fp32_str = fmt_memory(kws_fp32, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    kws_int8_str = fmt_memory(kws_int8, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    kws_train_str = fmt_memory(kws_train, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    flops_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple((resnet.inference_flops / mobilenet.inference_flops).to("").magnitude, precision=1, commas=False)
```

| **Workload**     |                    **Parameters**                    |                  **Forward FLOPs**                  |                 **Weights (FP32)**                 |                 **Weights (INT8)**                 |           **Training state (16 B/param)**           |
|:-----------------|:----------------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------:|:--------------------------------------------------:|:--------------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------:|
| **ResNet-50**    |  `{python} LighthouseFootprints.resnet_params_str`   |   `{python} LighthouseFootprints.resnet_gflop_str`  |  `{python} LighthouseFootprints.resnet_fp32_str`   |  `{python} LighthouseFootprints.resnet_int8_str`   |   `{python} LighthouseFootprints.resnet_train_str`  |
| **MobileNetV2**  | `{python} LighthouseFootprints.mobilenet_params_str` | `{python} LighthouseFootprints.mobilenet_mflop_str` | `{python} LighthouseFootprints.mobilenet_fp32_str` | `{python} LighthouseFootprints.mobilenet_int8_str` | `{python} LighthouseFootprints.mobilenet_train_str` |
| **KWS (DS-CNN)** |    `{python} LighthouseFootprints.kws_params_str`    |    `{python} LighthouseFootprints.kws_mflop_str`    |    `{python} LighthouseFootprints.kws_fp32_str`    |    `{python} LighthouseFootprints.kws_int8_str`    |    `{python} LighthouseFootprints.kws_train_str`    |

: **Lighthouse Operations and Bytes**: Forward-pass operations per input and the bytes each workload occupies as FP32 weights, INT8 weights, and full mixed-precision training state, so that every later measurement can be checked against what the workload must compute and move. Activations and runtime buffers are excluded. {#tbl-benchmarking-lighthouse-footprints tbl-colwidths="[18,15,16,16,16,19]"}

The table already separates the halves of the chapter. ResNet-50 does `{python} LighthouseFootprints.flops_ratio_mult_str` MobileNetV2's arithmetic per image, so its training benchmarks are about whether an accelerator sustains its rate; MobileNetV2's INT8 weights fit in a few megabytes, so its deployment benchmarks are about latency, sustained thermal state, and energy on a small board.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ MobileNetV2, the lighthouse model for edge latency, is established in @sec-network-architectures-efficient-architectures-keyword-spotting-0625.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: MobileNetV2 deployment validation lighthouse callout.
# │ Goal: INT8 compression ratio and accelerator vs host-CPU latency for the pipeline.
# │       Single source for the composite edge board's latencies; later cells read them.
from mlsysim import Models
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_FP32, BYTES_INT8, MB, ms
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_memory, check

class MobileNetLighthouseSetup:
    _mobilenet_v2 = Models.Vision.MobileNetV2
    accel_latency = 2 * ms  # scenario assumption: INT8 MobileNetV2 on the board's attached accelerator (labeled composite)
    cpu_int8_latency = 15 * ms  # scenario assumption: INT8 MobileNetV2 on the board's host CPU
    _mv2_size = _mobilenet_v2.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP32)
    _mv2_int8_size = _mobilenet_v2.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    _mv2_compress = (_mv2_size / _mv2_int8_size).to_base_units().magnitude

    check(_mv2_compress == 4.0, f"Expected 4x INT8 compression, got {_mv2_compress:.1f}x")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    mobilenet_v2_size_mb_str = fmt_memory(_mv2_size, unit=MB, commas=False)
    mobilenet_v2_int8_size_mb_str = fmt_memory(_mv2_int8_size, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    mobilenet_v2_compression_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(_mv2_compress, precision=0, commas=False)
    accel_latency_ms_str = fmt_time(accel_latency, ms, precision=0, commas=False)
    cpu_latency_ms_str = fmt_time(cpu_int8_latency, ms, precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {#lhs-benchmarking-mobilenet-deployment-validation .callout-lighthouse title="MobileNetV2 deployment validation"}

MobileNetV2 serves as the lighthouse example for validating the complete optimization pipeline. MobileNetV2 refines v1's depthwise separable design with inverted residuals and linear bottlenecks while maintaining a similar parameter scale [@sandler2018]. It exemplifies the deployment challenges where benchmarking determines success or failure: compression can reduce model size, hardware acceleration can reduce inference latency, and only benchmarking can determine whether those gains survive the full deployment pipeline.

1. **Model compression** (@sec-model-compression): INT8 quantization\index{Quantization!INT8 compression ratio} reduces this MobileNetV2 worked example from `{python} MobileNetLighthouseSetup.mobilenet_v2_size_mb_str` to `{python} MobileNetLighthouseSetup.mobilenet_v2_int8_size_mb_str` (`{python} MobileNetLighthouseSetup.mobilenet_v2_compression_ratio_mult_str` compression)
2. **Hardware acceleration** (@sec-hardware-acceleration): in this illustrative scenario the board's attached INT8 accelerator runs inference in `{python} MobileNetLighthouseSetup.accel_latency_ms_str` against `{python} MobileNetLighthouseSetup.cpu_latency_ms_str` on its host CPU
3. **Benchmarking validation**: Verify the pipeline delivers in practice

A systematic evaluation isolates the accelerator's latency from preprocessing and data transfer overhead, confirms INT8 quantization preserves accuracy on edge cases such as unusual lighting, and verifies that throughput holds on the camera trap's own frames rather than on curated ImageNet test images alone.

:::

Each stage of that pipeline arrives with a favorable number from its own chapter, such as a smaller model file or a faster kernel. The benchmarking question is which of those local numbers still hold once the stages run together on the target device, and three principles guide how the chapter answers it.

First, *benchmarks are proxies, not truth.*\index{Benchmarking!benchmarks as proxies} Every benchmark measures specific conditions that may not match the target deployment. A system can achieve high sample throughput in Offline mode (bulk throughput with all inputs available) and much lower queries per second (QPS) in Server mode (latency-constrained requests arriving over time). The critical question is always what the benchmark does not measure.

Second, Goodhart's Law governs benchmark rankings.[^fn-goodharts-law-metric]\index{Goodhart's law!metric trap} "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Teams that optimize for benchmark rankings often produce systems that excel in evaluation but fail in production. Benchmark-specific optimizations frequently degrade characteristics that matter for deployment: robustness, calibration, and efficiency.

Third, end-to-end beats component metrics\index{Benchmarking!end-to-end vs. component metrics}. A component speedup is diluted by every stage of the request it does not touch, and the dilution follows Amdahl's law; @sec-benchmarking-benchmarking-granularity-3855 quantifies it on a vision pipeline. These principles reappear throughout the methodology and return as misconceptions in @sec-benchmarking-fallacies-pitfalls-9781.

Two terms recur from here on. A service-level objective (SLO)\index{SLO!first use} is the target a deployed service commits to meet for a measured quantity, such as answering 99 percent of requests within a stated time; @sec-benchmarking-latency-tail-latency-5cde defines it formally. The 99th-percentile latency (p99)\index{P99!first use} is the response time that 99 percent of requests meet or beat, so it describes the slowest 1 percent of requests rather than the typical one.

[^fn-goodharts-law-metric]: **Goodhart's law**\index{Goodhart's law!etymology}: @goodhart1984 articulated the original 1975 Bank of England observation on monetary policy; @strathern1997improving generalized it into the form quoted above. The original context was macroeconomics: once a monetary aggregate became an official policy target, banks changed behavior to game the metric, destroying its predictive value. In ML, the same failure mode recurs structurally: BLEU rewards n-gram overlap [@papineni2001], ImageNet rewards performance on a fixed visual distribution [@deng2009; @recht2019imagenet], and benchmark leaderboards can incentivize test-set-specific tuning.

The chapter builds the measurement before it applies it (@tbl-benchmarking-chapter-spine). Benchmark carpentry turns a claim into a test that fixes the task, data, model, metrics, harness, and run rules. Granularity decides how much of the system a test spans, from one kernel to the whole request path, and it is where the roofline's prediction for ResNet-50 meets a measurement. Benchmark suites standardize those choices across organizations. The training and inference sections apply them to ResNet-50 and to MobileNetV2 on its edge board, and power measurement adds the joules, with keyword spotting as the case. Best practices supply the statistics that decide whether a measured difference is real, and model and data evaluation test the two dimensions that a hardware result cannot certify. The fallacies and the summary close by asking whether the evidence survives production traffic.

| **Section**                      | **Claim it tests**                                    | **What is measured**                                                      | **Granularity**                    | **Unit**               | **Trap it guards against**                                     |
|:---------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Benchmark Carpentry**          | ResNet-50 at INT8 is faster than at FP32              | The claim restated as task, data, model, metric, harness, and run rules   | Set by the claim                   | Stated per metric      | A number reported without its conditions                       |
| **Benchmarking Granularity**     | A kernel speedup speeds up the request                | Kernel, model, and request-path time; predicted against measured roofline | Micro, macro, end to end           | s, FLOP/s, B/s         | A component speedup diluted by untouched stages                |
| **Benchmark Suites**             | Two vendors' numbers are comparable                   | A reference workload under shared divisions, scenarios, and run rules     | Model and system                   | Time to quality, QPS   | Favorable conditions chosen separately by each vendor          |
| **Training Benchmarks**          | More accelerators train a model proportionally faster | Time to target accuracy, throughput, scaling efficiency, MFU              | Model on one to eight accelerators | s, images/s, percent   | Throughput that never reaches the quality target               |
| **Inference Benchmarks**         | MobileNetV2 meets its frame deadline on the board     | Latency percentiles, throughput, memory, cold start                       | End to end on one board            | ms (p50, p99), FPS, B  | A mean that hides the tail; a burst that hides throttling      |
| **Power and Energy Measurement** | The device lasts on its battery                       | Energy over a matched window; average power across the duty cycle         | Device or system boundary          | J per inference, W     | Efficiency quoted at an operating point the device never holds |
| **Benchmarking Best Practices**  | A measured difference is real                         | Repeated runs, paired tests, confidence intervals                         | Any                                | Interval               | A one-point gap inside sampling noise                          |
| **Model and Data Evaluation**    | The compressed model is still right on deployed data  | Confidence calibration, slices, coverage, label quality, shift            | Model and dataset                  | ECE, percent per slice | Aggregate accuracy that hides calibration and subgroup loss    |

: **Chapter Map**: Each section turns one optimization claim into a measurement, names the granularity and unit the measurement uses, and names the trap that a careless version of the measurement falls into. {#tbl-benchmarking-chapter-spine tbl-colwidths="[16,18,22,13,12,19]"}

Knowing *what* to measure is only half of the problem. Measuring incorrectly, with the wrong workload, a biased baseline, or an uncontrolled variable, produces numbers that look precise and mislead the decision they inform. The history of computing benchmarks[^fn-benchmark-etymology-surveying] is full of technically sound metrics applied with flawed methodology, from compiler-gamed Whetstone scores to throughput claims that predict nothing about sustained workloads (@sec-benchmarking-historical-context-7350). The defense is construction. A benchmark must be built so that it measures what its claim says, and that construction is where the chapter begins.

[^fn-benchmark-etymology-surveying]: **Benchmark**\index{Benchmark!etymology}: From surveying, where a "bench mark" was a horizontal cut in stone serving as a fixed elevation reference. The term entered computing in the 1970s to describe standardized comparison points, and the surveying metaphor carries a systems lesson. Just as an elevation measurement is meaningless without a calibrated reference, an ML throughput number is meaningless without controlled workloads, thermal state, and precision settings.

## Benchmark Carpentry {#sec-benchmarking-benchmark-components-97cc}

A claim that ResNet-50 runs faster at INT8 than at FP32 can reverse depending on whether timing starts at a JPEG on storage or at a preprocessed tensor in accelerator memory, or whether the quantized weights drop accuracy below the target floor. **Benchmark carpentry**\index{Benchmark carpentry!definition} is the craft of building a benchmark that measures what its claim says. It fixes the task, data, model, metrics, harness, system specification, and run rules so that the number the benchmark produces answers the engineering question and no other. A synthetic matrix-multiplication loop, a ResNet-50 training run over ImageNet, and a full serving pipeline all need these specifications, and changing one component changes what the next can measure. The components follow the D·A·M taxonomy. The problem definition fixes the input representation (Data). The dataset and task objective bound the feasible models (Algorithm). The target hardware's memory, energy envelope, and deadlines bound how the model may execute (Machine).

Evaluating an ML system requires coupling statistical task metrics with physical efficiency metrics. Quantization and pruning reduce parameter footprint and memory bus traffic, but they alter numerical representations and risk degrading task accuracy. A benchmark that records execution latency without statistical accuracy (such as area under the ROC curve (AUC) or classification error) rewards aggressive approximations that produce invalid outputs. Conversely, reporting accuracy without latency or memory consumption conceals whether the model satisfies the target system's physical constraints.

The measurement harness and run rules provide the experimental controls that make these evaluations reproducible. The protocol follows the question being tested. A controlled steady-state experiment can use warm-up iterations, fixed processor clocks, and pinned host memory to isolate execution differences. A deployment benchmark instead retains the relevant dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) policy, cold starts, and competing workloads, documenting their effects. Recording tail latency distributions (p95, p99) alongside the mean exposes delays hidden by averages. Each component is built here on the claim the chapter inherited, that ResNet-50 runs faster at INT8 than at FP32, and MLPerf Tiny's anomaly-detection benchmark at the end shows every component fixed at once on a small embedded model.

### Turning a claim into a test {#sec-benchmarking-problem-definition-79e4}

Every benchmark begins as a claim. The claim from the preceding chapters, that ResNet-50 at INT8 runs faster than at FP32 without unacceptable accuracy loss, is not yet testable, because it names neither the inputs, the output, nor the conditions under which faster must hold. Fixing those boundaries is the first act of carpentry. Without an explicit task specification, hardware and software optimizations cannot be evaluated on equivalent terms: altering an input resolution, a numerical datatype, or a latency deadline changes how much work the machine does. For ResNet-50 the input is a decoded $224{\times}224$ RGB image and the output is one of a thousand ImageNet class labels. Whether the task is natural language processing [@hirschberg2015] or computer vision [@everingham2009; @lin2014microsoft], a complete problem definition establishes three specifications: an input specification, an output specification, and a performance specification.

The input and output specifications fix the data each run must move and define the exact scope of timed execution. The input specification fixes tensor dimensions, batching behavior, numerical representations (such as FP16 or INT8), and ingestion rates. For the ResNet-50 claim, it decides whether timing starts at a JPEG on storage or at a preprocessed tensor already in accelerator memory, a choice that can change the measured time more than the precision change being tested. Conversely, the output specification defines the termination boundary of the computation. Benchmarks frequently introduce measurement bias by timing only accelerator forward passes while ignoring the CPU post-processing required to turn raw tensor outputs into usable decisions. A robust output specification defines whether the system emits raw logits, intermediate embeddings, or final class labels, accounting for any downstream thresholding or reduction kernels that consume host memory bandwidth.

The performance specification defines the operational envelope that governs whether an optimization is viable. Unconstrained throughput numbers are meaningless if statistical accuracy degrades below acceptable thresholds, and high average throughput cannot rescue a system that violates a latency service-level agreement (SLA). For the ResNet-50 claim, the performance specification couples a quality floor (MLPerf Training requires 75.9 percent top-1, and an INT8 deployment might permit at most one percentage point of loss against FP32) with hardware execution limits. These are a tail-latency ceiling, sustained throughput matching the arrival rate of images, and a resident memory footprint that leaves room for activations at the chosen batch size. By defining these three boundaries up front, the benchmark ensures that the later stages, from dataset construction to measurement harness configuration, evaluate system optimizations against the true operational constraints of deployment.

### Task and dataset {#sec-benchmarking-standardized-datasets-123f}

A task definition is only as rigorous as the data used to evaluate it. Standardized datasets enforce identical evaluation conditions across competing approaches, preventing teams from cherry-picking private slices that obscure comparative weaknesses. In computer vision, ImageNet\index{ImageNet!standardized dataset} [@imagenet_website; @deng2009], COCO\index{COCO!object detection dataset} [@lin2014microsoft], and CIFAR-10\index{CIFAR-10!classification reference dataset} [@cifar10_website] establish reference tasks across classification and detection. In natural language processing, SQuAD\index{SQuAD!reading comprehension dataset}[^fn-squad-question-answering] [@rajpurkar2016], GLUE\index{GLUE!language understanding benchmark}[^fn-glue-benchmark-saturation] [@wang2018], and WikiText [@wikitext_website; @merity2016pointer] fulfill equivalent roles by standardizing comprehension, classification, and language modeling across diverse textual domains.

[^fn-squad-question-answering]: **SQuAD (Stanford question answering dataset)**\index{SQuAD!saturation}: Introduced in 2016 with more than 100,000 question-answer pairs from Wikipedia [@rajpurkar2016]. AI systems exceeded the SQuAD 1.1 human baseline of 91.2 percent F1 by 2018 [@devlin2019], but the "superhuman" result reflects a benchmarking failure mode. The task's extractive format (answers are text spans within the passage) makes it easier than open-ended question answering, inflating perceived capability relative to production NLP systems.

[^fn-glue-benchmark-saturation]: **GLUE (general language understanding evaluation)**\index{GLUE!benchmark saturation}: Introduced in 2018 as a broad language-understanding benchmark [@wang2018], GLUE was quickly saturated by systems such as BERT [@devlin2019]. Once GLUE became a target, leaderboard optimization reduced its discriminating power, as Goodhart's Law predicts. The pattern motivated harder follow-on evaluations such as SuperGLUE and BIG-bench.

Dataset selection is the first place a benchmark can lose contact with deployment reality. ImageNet's validation set fixes ResNet-50's quality target, but its curated, centered photographs are not the frames a camera trap returns at dusk, a gap that @sec-benchmarking-data-benchmarking-22f9 returns to. A benchmark dataset must be representative enough to expose deployment failures and hard enough to separate models.

### Model and metrics {#sec-benchmarking-evaluation-metrics-6bac}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: bert-model-specs
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BERT MODEL SPECS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: BERT footnote in Model Selection section (~line 1334)
# │
# │ Goal: Provide BERT-Large parameter count for the BERT baseline footnote.
# │ Show: BERT-Large parameter count in millions.
# │ How: Retrieve from Models Digital Twin.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_params

class BertModelSpecs:
    """BERT-Large parameter count for the model selection footnote."""

    _bert_large_m = Models.Language.BERT_Large.parameters.to(Mparam).magnitude
    bert_large_params_m_str = fmt_params(Models.Language.BERT_Large.parameters, scale="M", precision=0, commas=False)
```

With the task and dataset fixed, the benchmark must specify the model architecture and its baseline implementations. In systems benchmarking, the model defines the execution workload. Its computational graph determines arithmetic intensity, memory footprint, and communication topology. Selecting the benchmark model determines whether measured performance variations reflect architectural efficiency, software runtime optimizations, or raw accelerator capacity. Evaluating an architectural modification requires holding the runtime and hardware target constant. Conversely, evaluating hardware platforms or software execution engines requires standardizing on a fixed, representative model graph so that throughput differences isolate execution efficiency rather than mathematical changes to the workload.

Baseline models\index{Baseline model!reference point selection} establish the empirical reference point for a target domain. Rather than toy algorithms, systems benchmarks rely on canonical workloads whose computational profiles and memory access patterns are well-characterized. In vision, ResNet-50 plays this role, which is why the chapter's claim is stated on it. In language processing, BERT[^fn-bert-benchmark-evaluation] serves as a standard baseline because its multi-head self-attention and dense feed-forward blocks exercise both compute-bound matrix multiplications and memory-bandwidth-bound reduction operations. However, a baseline specification cannot stop at the mathematical graph. Two implementations of the identical architecture across different frameworks or runtimes often behave differently at runtime. Differences in kernel fusion (such as fusing normalization and activation functions directly into general matrix multiply (GEMM) output epilogues to avoid round-trips to high-bandwidth memory (HBM)), kernel launch overhead, and memory allocator behavior can exceed the performance impact of minor architectural variations. A comparison that isolates hardware must control the runtime implementation alongside the mathematical model. A runtime comparison instead names that implementation as the intervention and documents both stacks.

[^fn-bert-benchmark-evaluation]: **BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers)**\index{BERT!benchmarking baseline}: BERT-Large (`{python} BertModelSpecs.bert_large_params_m_str` parameters) is a language-processing workload in MLPerf Inference. The benchmark fixes the task, data, quality target, and applicable execution scenarios so systems can be compared on the same workload. BERT latency still depends on sequence length, batching, and implementation.

A benchmark must select the operational regime relevant to its engineering question. In training, memory capacity and interconnect bandwidth can be binding constraints, because storing forward activations, backward gradients, and optimizer states across multiple accelerators limits batch size and demands high-bandwidth collective communication. Training benchmarks therefore measure time-to-accuracy under fixed convergence criteria rather than raw iteration speed alone. In inference, backward passes and optimizer states disappear. Evaluation instead emphasizes the serving objective, such as tail latency under SLAs, while low-batch autoregressive decode often faces bandwidth pressure. Transitioning a model to production frequently requires precision reduction, quantizing FP32 or BF16 weights and activations to INT8 or FP8. Moving eligible tensors from a 16-bit to an 8-bit format halves their raw storage and can reduce traffic or raise supported arithmetic throughput. Whole-model gains depend on the execution path, and validation must establish whether numerical error stays within the quality target. A development-to-deployment comparison may need both regimes because efficient training does not establish serving feasibility; a deployment decision for a fixed pretrained model can focus on inference.

Evaluation metrics[^fn-metric-etymology-measurement] translate raw model behavior into numbers that can be compared, ranked, and used to make engineering decisions. The difficulty lies in choosing the right numbers. A metric that captures accuracy but ignores latency may declare the winner to be a model too slow for production; one that rewards throughput but ignores energy may optimize for a deployment budget that does not exist. @Tbl-metric-taxonomy categorizes evaluation measures by the failure mode each exposes and the deployment context it serves. <!-- {#sec-benchmarking-metric-taxonomy-d4cd} -->

[^fn-metric-etymology-measurement]: **Metric**\index{Metric!etymology}\index{Metric!intransitivity}: In mathematics, a metric is a distance function satisfying strict axioms including the triangle inequality. ML borrows the term loosely for quantitative measures such as BLEU and perplexity, which are scoring rules rather than mathematical metrics. Leaderboard rankings can change when the evaluation protocol, dataset slice, or metric weighting changes, making the choice of metric an engineering decision that shapes which system wins, not just how performance is measured.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}
```

| **Category**   | **Metric**                   | **Unit**               | **Primary Use Case**   |
|:---------------|:-----------------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Accuracy**   | Top-1/Top-5 Accuracy         | Percentage             | Classification         |
|                | mAP (mean Average Precision) | 0–1 score              | Object detection       |
|                | BLEU/ROUGE                   | 0–100 score            | NLP generation         |
|                | Perplexity                   | Score (lower = better) | Language modeling      |
| **Throughput** | Samples/second               | Samples/s              | Batch inference        |
|                | Token throughput             | tokens/s               | LLM inference          |
|                | Time-to-train                | Hours/days             | Training benchmarks    |
| **Latency**    | p50 latency                  | Milliseconds           | Median response time   |
|                | p99 latency                  | Milliseconds           | Tail latency (SLA)     |
|                | First-token latency          | Milliseconds           | LLM responsiveness     |
| **Efficiency** | Samples/second/watt          | Samples/s/W            | Energy efficiency      |
|                | Accuracy/FLOP                | percent/PFLOP          | Algorithmic efficiency |
|                | TCO per inference            | \$/inference           | Economic efficiency    |

: **ML Benchmarking Metric Taxonomy**: Metrics organized by evaluation category, unit, and primary use case. Accuracy metrics quantify model quality, throughput and latency metrics capture system speed, and efficiency metrics combine multiple dimensions. Selecting the right metric for the deployment context is often more important than optimizing any single metric to its maximum. {#tbl-metric-taxonomy}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

The metrics in @tbl-metric-taxonomy expose physical trade-offs governed by the accelerator architecture. Throughput\index{Throughput!vs. latency trade-off} measures aggregate processing capacity, whereas latency\index{Latency!percentile, p50 p95 p99 reporting} measures individual request completion time. These two objectives conflict directly at the hardware boundary. Maximizing throughput requires aggregating requests into larger batches to amortize weight-loading memory bandwidth across multiple inputs, raising arithmetic intensity on tensor units. That batching mechanism inflates per-sample latency, because individual requests wait in arrival queues while a batch forms, and larger matrix operations take longer to complete. Furthermore, arithmetic mean latency masks tail behavior. Queuing jitter, memory allocation stalls, and accelerator thermal throttling cause execution times to diverge; a system with a 10 ms mean latency can still suffer a 500 ms p99 latency that violates service-level agreements. Benchmarks must therefore report distribution percentiles (p50, p95, p99) rather than averages. Compound metrics such as samples/second/watt compress multiple dimensions into a single scalar, simplifying high-level comparisons but obscuring where bottlenecks reside. Reporting atomic metrics (latency distributions, throughput, and power draw) alongside compound figures isolates which physical constraint limits the system.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The batch size at which waiting for a batch to form pushes latency past its budget is measured with a batch-size sweep in @sec-model-serving-batching-tax.
:::

Task-specific metrics evaluate the algorithmic dimension, quantifying whether the model solves the statistical problem. Classification workloads evaluate accuracy (the fraction of correct predictions), precision\index{Precision!positive prediction accuracy}, recall\index{Recall!positive case detection rate}, and the F1 score\index{F1 score!precision-recall harmonic mean} [@sokolova2009]. Precision and recall isolate true positive rates from false alarms, which is essential when class distributions are imbalanced. Continuous estimation tasks rely on Mean Squared Error (MSE) or Mean Absolute Error (MAE), while sequence generation uses specialized scoring rules such as BLEU[^fn-bleu-score-translation] to measure modified n-gram precision against human reference translations [@papineni2001].

[^fn-bleu-score-translation]: **BLEU (bilingual evaluation understudy)**\index{BLEU!Goodhart's law example}: Introduced by IBM in 2002, BLEU measures translation quality through modified n-gram precision with a brevity penalty against reference translations [@papineni2001]. BLEU is a canonical example of Goodhart's Law in ML, because optimizing for n-gram matches can reward surface-level word overlap even when meaning, fluency, or deployment usefulness diverges from the target.

Task metrics evaluate algorithmic quality in isolation, but deployment viability depends on physical machine constraints. Model capacity, measured in parameter count and memory footprint, determines whether weights fit into on-chip SRAM or accelerator memory, or whether they spill across high-latency interconnects. Per-inference execution latency dictates whether a system meets real-time deadlines, while energy consumption per inference (measured in joules or millijoules) bounds thermal dissipation and battery life.

Benchmarks must also account for measurement sensitivity across software runtimes. As established in @sec-model-training, different frameworks handle loss computation, kernel fusion, and gradient accumulation differently, altering reported benchmark numbers. Subtle implementation differences shift measured accuracy and latency enough to invert benchmark rankings when candidate models differ by narrow margins. Examples include whether batch normalization is configured to use stored running statistics or current mini-batch statistics during evaluation, and how reduction kernels reorder non-associative floating-point additions.

### Benchmark harness {#sec-benchmarking-benchmark-harness-09ea}

Metrics define *what* to measure; the benchmark harness\index{Benchmark harness!test infrastructure} determines *how* to measure it. The harness is the software and instrumentation scaffold that feeds inputs to the system under test, coordinates execution, collects timing and power traces, and enforces reproducibility\index{Reproducibility!benchmark requirement}. In an ML system, measuring execution down to the metal requires accounting for the asynchronous execution boundary between the host CPU and the accelerator. When host software initiates an inference or training step, the framework runtime merely enqueues commands onto an accelerator work queue (such as a CUDA stream or hardware command buffer) and returns control immediately. A naive timer wrapping the host-level call measures only this sub-microsecond queue dispatch latency rather than actual device execution. A rigorous harness inserts explicit device synchronization barriers (such as `torch.cuda.synchronize()`) or queries on-device timestamp events (such as `torch.cuda.Event`), ensuring that recorded timings cover the declared device-work interval rather than mere host enqueue overhead.

The timer endpoints determine which work enters the result. @Fig-benchmark-async-timing separates the host call, the synchronized host interval, and the device-event interval for one inference.

::: {#fig-benchmark-async-timing fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Timing Across an Asynchronous Boundary**: The host call returns after enqueueing work, before the accelerator completes it. A synchronized host timer spans enqueueing through completion; device events measure elapsed time between their positions on the stream. The timing boundaries determine whether transfers and other queued work are included." fig-alt="Two aligned host and accelerator lanes with an enqueue block, a host waiting block, and an accelerator work block. Three arrows mark the call timer, the device-event interval, and the synchronized host interval."}

These intervals answer different questions. Earlier device work must finish before the host timer starts. A synchronized host interval then measures elapsed completion time under the stated synchronization boundary, whereas events measure the interval between their positions in the accelerator stream. A report must state those boundaries before comparing two implementations; neither method includes work that falls outside them.

Harness architecture must align with the operational regime of the deployment target. In server environments, the harness generates concurrent request traffic using an open-loop load generator, often parameterizing inter-arrival times with a Poisson distribution.[^fn-poisson-arrival-benchmark] An open-loop harness issues requests according to an independent arrival schedule regardless of server responsiveness. This decoupling exposes queuing delays and tail latency (such as p99 response times) when arrival bursts saturate available compute.

In contrast, a naive benchmarking client often employs a closed-loop pattern: sending a request, blocking until the response arrives, and only then issuing the next request. This design introduces the severe measurement distortion known as **coordinated omission**\index{Coordinated omission!closed-loop measurement trap}. Consider a server that experiences a transient 500 ms garbage collection pause or memory reallocation stall. In an open-loop production environment, independent users continue submitting queries, causing dozens of requests to accumulate in the server's ingress queue; once the pause ends, every queued query suffers inflated tail latency. In a closed-loop benchmark, however, the client blocks idly during the entire 500 ms pause, sending zero traffic while the server is struggling. The benchmark records a single slow query and zero queue backlog. By coordinating request generation with server responsiveness, the closed-loop harness artificially paces traffic, systematically erasing the very queue collapse and p99 latency spikes it was constructed to measure.

The missing requests are the source of the distortion. @Fig-benchmark-coordinated-omission aligns the two arrival policies against one server pause so that the change in offered work remains visible.

::: {#fig-benchmark-coordinated-omission fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**A Pause Under Two Arrival Policies**: Each green interval runs from a request arrival to its response. Independent arrivals continue through the same server pause, while one closed-loop client waits for a response before sending again. The resulting workloads differ, so the closed-loop sample omits delays that the independent stream would experience. The timeline is schematic." fig-alt="Aligned request timelines under one shaded server pause. Four open-loop requests arrive during the pause, while a closed-loop client sends one request during the pause and its next request after the response."}

A closed-loop result is valid for a population whose clients wait in this way. It does not by itself estimate latency for an independent arrival stream, because it reduces the offered load precisely when the server slows. The harness must therefore reproduce the deployment arrival policy or report why a different policy answers the intended question.

Offline batch processing eliminates arrival scheduling entirely; the harness pre-stages large input batches in memory to saturate accelerator execution units, maximize memory bandwidth utilization, and measure peak sustained throughput.

[^fn-poisson-arrival-benchmark]: **Poisson distribution**\index{Poisson distribution!traffic modeling}: Named after Siméon Denis Poisson, who formalized it in 1837 while modeling wrongful conviction rates in French courts. The distribution models independent events at a constant average rate $(\ArrivalRate)$ and is a common baseline for server request arrivals. Real ML serving traffic often violates its assumptions through burstiness, correlation, and time-varying rates. A Poisson harness can therefore misestimate tail latency unless traces or stress cases cover those production patterns.

In embedded and edge deployments, workloads are neither stochastic network streams nor unconstrained batch queues. Instead, inputs arrive sequentially from physical sensors (such as an audio analog-to-digital converter or an image sensor) governed by fixed hardware sampling clocks. The harness must inject these sensor streams through direct memory access into limited on-chip SRAM buffers, verifying that each inference completes within the inter-sample arrival deadline to prevent buffer overflow. Furthermore, edge harnesses must integrate physical instrumentation, such as shunt resistors or external power analyzers, to sample voltage and current across active execution cycles and low-power sleep states, capturing the true energy consumed per inference.

Reproducibility requires specifying which runtime and environmental conditions are controlled and which are part of the workload. Warm-up matters at every scale, from a single kernel to a whole run, because modern accelerators and runtime frameworks have substantial cold-start transients. Initial inference passes trigger on-demand memory allocations, dynamic just-in-time (JIT) compilation, driver initialization, and weight transfers from secondary storage into accelerator memory. For steady-state measurements, the harness executes unmeasured warm-up iterations until caches populate, memory allocators stabilize, and the intended thermal operating state is reached. Controlled experiments may fix clocks and remove competing processes; deployment tests retain and report the relevant DVFS policy and contention. Cold-start measurements time initialization separately instead of discarding it. Finally, telemetry logging must minimize the probe effect by recording execution timestamps and performance counters into non-blocking, pre-allocated memory buffers. The remaining instrumentation overhead should be checked against a minimally instrumented run.

### Specifications and run rules {#sec-benchmarking-run-rules-c33f}

Complementing the harness that controls execution conditions, system specifications record the computational environment, the physical hardware and software stack that establishes the Machine ($\text{M}$) boundaries of the system. Run rules govern how the benchmark runs on it. Without both, a reported throughput or latency measurement cannot be interpreted. An execution metric reflects the interaction between an algorithm's arithmetic intensity and a machine's physical limits: peak arithmetic throughput, memory hierarchy bandwidth, and interconnect latency. A throughput figure reported without accelerator model, memory bandwidth, or operating clocks conceals whether an observed speedup stems from algorithmic efficiency or upgraded silicon. A result reported without its seed policy conceals whether it is reproducible at all, because the stochastic processes catalogued in @sec-benchmarking-ml-measurement-challenges-60ea mean that two runs on identical hardware can produce different numbers. A protocol may fix seeds and data order when isolating system effects, or require repeated runs and quality thresholds when stochastic variation is part of the workload. @Tbl-benchmarking-spec-run-rules lists what a reproducible report records.

| **Item**                       | **What the report records**                                                                | **Why the result depends on it**                                          |
|:-------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Accelerator**                | Microarchitecture, active core count, base and boost clocks, power limit (TDP)             | Sets the peak arithmetic rate and how long boost clocks persist           |
| **Device memory**              | Capacity, bus width, peak bandwidth                                                        | Sets the bandwidth ceiling and the largest batch that fits                |
| **Multi-accelerator topology** | Host interface (PCIe lanes) and accelerator links (NVLink or shared PCIe switches)         | All-reduce time is bounded by link bandwidth and topology                 |
| **Software stack**             | Operating system, driver, compute runtime (CUDA or ROCm), math libraries (cuBLAS, CUTLASS) | Kernel selection, tiling, and reduction order change with library version |
| **Framework layer**            | Framework version, eager or compiled execution (`torch.compile`), fusion settings          | Separates framework overhead from model cost                              |
| **Power and thermal**          | Sustained board power, throttling events, energy per sample or token                       | A speedup from transient clock boosting does not persist                  |
| **Randomness**                 | Seed policy, data order, known nondeterministic kernels                                    | Two runs on identical hardware can produce different numbers              |
| **Configuration**              | Every hyperparameter, including the learning-rate schedule                                 | A learning-rate change shifts convergence and final accuracy              |
| **Data**                       | Dataset version, splits, preprocessing; any privacy or licensing limit on sharing          | Different splits or preprocessing define a different workload             |
| **Code**                       | Version of model, preprocessing, training, and evaluation code; container image            | Lets another team inspect and, where access permits, reproduce the run    |

: **Benchmark Specification and Run Rules**: What a reproducible benchmark report records about the machine, the software, and the run, and why each item changes the measured result. {#tbl-benchmarking-spec-run-rules tbl-colwidths="[18,46,36]"}

Reference suites may distribute containerized environments that encapsulate dependencies and configurations, while experimental logs retain training metrics, checkpoints, and any mid-run adjustments. Together, these records turn a one-time measurement into evidence another team can inspect and, when access permits, reproduce.

### Interpreting results {#sec-benchmarking-result-interpretation-cd29}

Producing raw benchmark numbers requires only execution. Interpreting them requires understanding the conditions that produced them, the statistical confidence behind them, and the operational boundaries that determine whether the numbers translate to production behavior. A single reported metric, such as latency or accuracy, rarely reveals whether an optimization succeeds in deployment. <!-- {#sec-benchmarking-benchmark-result-interpretation-framework-16a7} -->

Translating benchmark numbers into engineering decisions requires two methodological checks: a defined intervention and statistical rigor. First, state what changes and what remains comparable. ResNet-50 versus MobileNet can be a valid architecture comparison at matched task and quality requirements; FP32 versus INT8 can be a valid precision comparison on a supported execution path. Hold the other relevant conditions fixed or report their changes, including batch size, hardware, runtime, input distribution, and service targets. Second, distinguish steady-state execution from initialization, using the harness's warm-up protocol (@sec-benchmarking-benchmark-harness-09ea). A single run conflates cold-start overhead (kernel compilation, page faults, and cache warming) with sustained throughput, while a prolonged stress test may instead capture the thermal throttling examined for edge devices in @sec-benchmarking-mobile-edge-benchmarks-fd4f. Report cold-start and steady-state results according to the deployment question, and record variation across repeated trials. Whether a measured difference exceeds that variation is a statistical question, answered with the interval and paired-test rules of @sec-benchmarking-statistical-methodological-issues-7aa5.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Interpreting a benchmark claim callout (H100 TDP).
# │ Goal: H100 TDP for a complete vendor-specification example.
from mlsysim import Hardware
from mlsysim.core.units import watt
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_count, fmt_power

class H100TdpClaim:
    vendor_claim_ips = 10_000
    spec_batch_size = 32
    spec_top1_pct = 76

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    vendor_claim_ips_str = fmt_count(vendor_claim_ips, commas=True, label="inference")
    spec_batch_size_str = fmt(spec_batch_size, precision=0, commas=False)
    spec_top1_pct_str = fmt_percent(spec_top1_pct / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    h100_tdp_w_str = fmt_power(Hardware.Cloud.H100.tdp, unit=watt, precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {#psp-benchmarking-interpreting-benchmark-claim .callout-perspective title="Interpreting a benchmark claim"}

A vendor claims "Our system achieves `{python} H100TdpClaim.vendor_claim_ips_str`/second on ResNet-50." Taken alone, the number cannot support deployment planning because the conditions that determine its meaning are unstated.

Four unstated conditions determine what the claim means:

1. **Batch size**: Large batches amortize weight transfers and maximize compute utilization but inflate queuing delay; batch 1 minimizes latency but leaves execution units underutilized.
2. **Precision**: INT8 execution exploits higher-throughput integer pipelines and cuts memory traffic, but requires quantization-range calibration that can compromise numerical fidelity.
3. **Measurement boundary**: The measurement window must state whether it isolates pure accelerator kernel execution or includes host-to-device transfers, JPEG decoding, and tensor format conversions.
4. **Accuracy**: The claim must state whether the optimized model retains baseline validation accuracy (such as 76.1 percent Top-1 on ImageNet) or trades task quality for raw execution speed.

**Example**: "`{python} H100TdpClaim.vendor_claim_ips_str`/second on ResNet-50 at batch size `{python} H100TdpClaim.spec_batch_size_str`, INT8 precision, `{python} H100TdpClaim.spec_top1_pct_str` Top-1 accuracy, including JPEG decoding, on NVIDIA H100 at `{python} H100TdpClaim.h100_tdp_w_str` thermal design power (TDP)."

**Systems insight**: A throughput figure lacking batch size, precision, measurement scope, and accuracy targets is a marketing metric rather than an engineering specification.

:::

A claim whose workload boundary, precision, and excluded costs cannot be reconstructed should be rejected. Marketing phrases compress such omissions into a few words, usually reporting the most favorable operating point without saying so. @Tbl-benchmarking-vendor-claims translates common ones into the technical caveats behind each.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.4}
```

| **Vendor Claim**               | **What It Often Means**                                            |
|:-------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **"Up to 10,000 images/sec"**  | Peak throughput at maximum batch size, INT8, without preprocessing |
| **"Sub-millisecond latency"**  | Accelerator compute only, excluding data transfer                  |
| **"5$\times$ more efficient"** | Per-operation efficiency, not total system efficiency              |
| **"Optimized for AI"**         | May only accelerate specific operations or precisions              |

: **Decoding Vendor Benchmark Claims**: Four common marketing phrases and the technical caveats that determine whether a claim describes end-to-end performance, a narrow accelerator measurement, or an unsupported efficiency comparison. {#tbl-benchmarking-vendor-claims}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

Which metric governs viability depends on the deployment. In safety-critical applications such as medical imaging or autonomous driving, a 1 percent accuracy gain justifies substantial computational cost. In interactive search or speech transcription, tail latency within a tight service-level agreement dominates, so a minor accuracy gain is irrelevant if it breaches the latency budget. Systems evaluation must also guard against *benchmark overfitting*, in which an optimization targets the idiosyncratic computational patterns of a standardized suite at the expense of production workloads. For example, aggressive kernel fusion or operator tiling tuned exclusively for fixed sequence lengths in a benchmark harness can degrade throughput when deployed against dynamic, variable-length user requests. Robust interpretation requires validating performance across diverse input distributions, perturbed batch sizes, and representative operational duty cycles.

::: {#chk-benchmarking-vendor-claims .callout-checkpoint title="Decoding vendor benchmark claims"}

When evaluating hardware or software based on vendor-reported benchmarks, check whether the claim identifies the workload, measurement boundary, and operating conditions.

- [ ] Measured quantity: Does the latency number include preprocessing and postprocessing, not just model execution?
- [ ] Precision boundary: Can the precision behind a throughput claim, such as INT4 versus INT8 or FP16, be identified?
- [ ] Workload boundary: Are the model, batch size, and input distribution used to produce the comparison explicitly named?
- [ ] Excluded costs: Are memory transfers, model loading, initialization, sustained thermal behavior, and power accounted for at the claimed performance level?
- [ ] Claimed vs. achieved: Given a 1,000 TFLOP/s peak claim and a benchmark that sustains 350 TFLOP/s, estimate the MFU and state whether that utilization ratio alone identifies the bottleneck.

:::

### A complete reference benchmark {#sec-benchmarking-example-benchmark-229f}

MLPerf Tiny's anomaly-detection benchmark shows every component fixed at once on one small embedded model. The multi-stage pipeline in @fig-benchmark-components traces this industrial audio benchmark across nine sequential phases. It carries the task from problem definition in the top chevrons through spectrogram extraction, autoencoder training, and INT8 quantization down to embedded deployment on an ARM mbed OS microcontroller. Each stage fixes boundary conditions for the next. The problem definition dictates the acoustic sampling rate and input representation (Data). The dataset properties and task objective determine feasible model architectures (Algorithm). The microcontroller's hardware limits (SRAM capacity, energy envelope, and real-time latency deadlines) dictate INT8 quantization and memory-efficient kernel compilation (Machine). Here every choice constrains the next, so a benchmark that measures only classification accuracy or only raw inference latency misses cross-stage interactions, where an engineering decision at any stage narrows the feasible design space downstream.
