While @sec-benchmarking-model-benchmarking-4847 evaluates model compression against task accuracy baselines, system benchmarking isolates the execution efficiency of the hardware-software stack under a fixed model. Modern accelerators rarely sustain theoretical peak throughput because physical execution depends on the coupling between tensor shapes and memory hierarchies. ResNet-50 training, which the roofline places on the compute roof, sustains about `{python} ResNet50H100Sustained.mfu_pct_str` of an H100's peak (notebook \ref{nbk-benchmarking-resnet50-roofline-vs-measured}). Parameter-heavy transformer decodes and activation-heavy convolutional passes stress entirely different levels of the memory subsystem, causing achievable throughput to diverge across precision formats.

Measuring sustained utilization rather than peak capability establishes two critical scope boundaries. First, energy consumption scales with execution efficiency, because performance per watt varies widely across hardware platforms, and an underutilized accelerator draws substantial static power for minimal computational output. Second, multi-accelerator execution introduces communication boundaries. While multi-node cluster scaling involves network-topology effects beyond this book's single-node scope, intra-node benchmarking must account for interconnect bandwidth, memory sharing across accelerators, and gradient synchronization over NVLink or PCIe.

### Community-driven standardization {#sec-benchmarking-communitydriven-standardization-5c56}

Without shared measurement boundaries, utilization numbers cannot be compared. If one benchmark includes host-side preprocessing and PCIe transfers while another measures only device kernel execution, or if one power meter reads only the accelerator voltage rail while another includes host processors and chassis fans, the resulting figures reflect incompatible boundaries rather than architectural efficiency. No single vendor can resolve this discrepancy, because each has a commercial incentive to draw the boundary around its own hardware strengths. Formal standards bodies move too slowly for hardware and model structures that change every year, so consortia such as MLCommons maintain living benchmark suites. These pair open-source reference implementations with compliance rules so that numbers from different laboratories describe comparable workloads under the same version, division, quality target, and scenario.

Standardizing system benchmarks requires formalizing the D·A·M taxonomy so that evaluations isolate the Machine without confounding changes to the Algorithm or Data. The MLPerf Training benchmark enforces this separation by measuring time-to-train to a specified quality target rather than raw floating-point throughput or epoch duration [@mattson2020mlperf]. High TFLOP/s from aggressive low-precision scaling helps only if faster steps outweigh any extra work needed to reach the target, and a run that misses the target is invalid. MLPerf splits submissions into two divisions. In the closed division\index{Closed division!MLPerf training}, every submitter must run the reference model and reach the same quality target, so differences in time-to-train belong to the system. The open division permits model and algorithm changes, so its results compare whole solutions rather than machines. Within the closed division, the rules constrain the workload while permitting specified tunable hyperparameters and approved numerical formats. Quality and compliance checks establish which hardware, compiler, and training-configuration improvements constitute valid submissions.

The MLPerf Inference benchmark applies this discipline to production deployment constraints [@reddi2020]. An accelerator cannot simply report peak throughput under infinite batching if interactive serving requires guaranteed responsiveness. The benchmark therefore fixes how queries arrive, through execution scenarios matched to physical operating regimes: one query at a time for a single interactive user, randomly arriving queries under a tail-latency bound for a shared service, and all inputs supplied upfront for bulk throughput. By standardizing these execution boundaries, community benchmarks account for queueing delays and host-to-device PCIe transfers, making the tested load and timing boundary explicit when interpreting a throughput claim.

#### MLPerf execution scenarios {#sec-benchmarking-mlperf-execution-scenarios-89f0}

The same hardware can report dramatically different benchmark numbers depending on *how* requests arrive, which explains why vendor claims often fail to predict production performance. Classic MLPerf Inference defines four execution scenarios that characterize distinct traffic patterns, each requiring different optimization strategies [@reddi2020]. Current client and generative-AI benchmark variants also include interactive measurements for latency-sensitive large language model (LLM) workloads, where time to first token and time per output token, the two measured quantities defined in @sec-benchmarking-token-latency-ttft-tpot-4e1a, become central [@mlperf_client_website].

##### SingleStream {#sec-benchmarking-singlestream-c709}

SingleStream\index{SingleStream!sequential inference scenario} processes one request at a time, measuring latency for sequential inference. This scenario models mobile and embedded applications where a single user interacts with the device: a smartphone camera app classifying images, a voice assistant processing speech, or a wearable detecting gestures. The key metric is a tail percentile of per-query latency (the 90th percentile in MLPerf's rules), and inter-request batching is unavailable because the next query arrives after the previous one completes. Optimization focuses on preprocessing efficiency and power consumption rather than throughput.

##### MultiStream {#sec-benchmarking-multistream-38d1}

MultiStream\index{MultiStream!synchronized sensor fusion} processes multiple synchronized input streams simultaneously, modeling scenarios like autonomous vehicles with multiple cameras that must be processed together for spatial fusion. The application motivation is synchronized processing, but the benchmark rule is version-specific: current MultiStream rules issue a group of samples per query, wait for its completion before the next query, and report a specified latency percentile. Earlier versions used fixed arrival intervals. Grouped-query latency helps assess multi-input execution; it does not establish a hard-deadline guarantee for a vehicle planning loop.

##### Server {#sec-benchmarking-server-e69f}

Server\index{Server scenario!Poisson-distributed traffic} generates requests following a Poisson distribution, simulating cloud API traffic where requests arrive independently and unpredictably. This scenario models web services handling millions of queries from different users. Unlike SingleStream's guaranteed sequential arrival, Server traffic creates queuing dynamics where multiple requests compete for resources. The key metrics are throughput (queries per second) and the workload's tail-latency bound, typically set at the 99th percentile, and dynamic batching can improve efficiency by grouping requests that arrive within a time window. Optimization balances throughput against latency SLOs.

##### Offline {#sec-benchmarking-offline-6ece}

Offline\index{Offline scenario!maximum throughput mode} provides all inputs upfront, measuring maximum throughput when latency constraints are removed. This scenario models batch processing pipelines: overnight data processing, scientific computing, or precomputing recommendations. With no per-query latency requirement, systems can tune batch size for sustained throughput within memory and execution limits. The key metric is pure throughput (samples per second), and optimization focuses entirely on hardware efficiency. @Tbl-mlperf-scenarios maps the classic execution scenarios, plus the newer Interactive LLM-oriented case, to their deployment contexts and optimization strategies.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
```

| **Scenario**     | **Context**                         | **Strategy**                         | **Focus**                                  |
|:-----------------|:------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|
| **SingleStream** | Mobile apps, embedded devices       | No batching (batch = 1)              | Preprocessing, power efficiency            |
| **MultiStream**  | Autonomous driving, video analytics | Synchronized sensor fusion           | Grouped-query latency percentile           |
| **Server**       | Cloud APIs, web services            | Dynamic batching with timeout        | Throughput-latency trade-off tuning        |
| **Offline**      | Batch processing, data pipelines    | Maximum batch size                   | Throughput, hardware utilization           |
| **Interactive**  | Chat, agents, local generative AI   | Token streaming, KV-cache management | Time-to-first-token, time-per-output-token |

: **MLPerf Execution Scenarios**: Classic MLPerf Inference scenarios map to distinct deployment contexts, each requiring different optimization strategies, and newer Interactive scenarios extend the framework to latency-sensitive LLM workloads. SingleStream and MultiStream prioritize latency, Server balances throughput and latency, Offline maximizes throughput, and Interactive emphasizes token-level responsiveness. Matching the scenario to deployment context determines which benchmark results are relevant. {#tbl-mlperf-scenarios tbl-colwidths="[12,28,28,32]"}

Community standards fix the workload, the divisions, and the arrival pattern. The training and inference sections apply those rules to the chapter's lighthouse workloads, beginning with the one that consumes the most arithmetic per result: training ResNet-50 to its quality target.

## Training Benchmarks {#sec-benchmarking-training-benchmarks-96da}

Training and inference fail in opposite ways on the same accelerator. A training run stalls when synchronizing gradients across accelerators saturates the interconnect; a serving deployment violates its SLO when request bursts build a queue. The two regimes also measure different resources. Training iteratively refines parameters over billions of samples and must hold parameters, gradients, optimizer state, and the activations retained for the backward pass, a footprint that can far exceed the weights alone (@tbl-benchmarking-lighthouse-footprints gives ResNet-50's). Its figure of merit is wall-clock time to a target accuracy. Inference evaluates fixed parameters against arriving queries, discards the backward graph and optimizer state, and is judged by latency percentiles and throughput under bursty load. A training result and an inference result on the same accelerator therefore measure different resources and cannot stand in for each other, which is why MLPerf maintains separate Training and Inference suites [@mattson2020mlperf; @reddi2020]. This chapter measures training on ResNet-50 and serving on MobileNetV2 (@sec-benchmarking-inference-benchmarks-2c1f).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The training memory budget of weights, gradients, optimizer state, and retained activations is established in @sec-model-training-optimizer-memory-training-loop-4383.
:::

In an illustrative procurement failure, a team purchases a larger GPU cluster expecting proportional training-speed gains, only to discover that communication overhead and memory bottlenecks limit the actual speedup. Training benchmarks\index{ML training benchmark!convergence throughput scalability} exist to catch this kind of gap before procurement. Training benchmarks span six dimensions (@tbl-training-metrics), anchored by three: convergence metrics that measure learning progress, throughput metrics that measure computational efficiency, and scalability metrics that measure distributed performance.

::: {#dfn-benchmarking-ml-training-benchmarks .callout-definition title="ML training benchmarks"}

***ML training benchmarks***\index{ML training benchmark!definition} are machine learning system benchmarks that measure the time to reach a target quality metric (for example, a specified validation accuracy or loss threshold) on a fixed dataset and model, quantifying the rate of convergence per unit of resource.

1.  **Significance**: Training benchmarks reveal large gaps invisible to hardware specs. Holding the model and quality target fixed, the time to convergence can vary widely across hardware-software stacks because training performance depends on the full pipeline: data loading $(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)$, compute utilization $(\EfficiencyHw)$, gradient synchronization $(\Bandwidth, \Latency)$, and fault recovery overhead. A peak FLOP/s spec sheet captures none of these interactions.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike inference benchmarks, which measure per-query latency and throughput under load, training benchmarks measure time-to-accuracy across the full optimization loop: data loading, forward pass, backward pass, gradient synchronization, and optimizer step. As scale increases, communication $(\Bandwidth)$ can displace compute $(\PeakRate)$ as the binding constraint; profiling establishes the transition for a particular workload.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that training benchmarks measure "how fast the GPU runs." At large scale, interconnect bandwidth $(\Bandwidth)$ for gradient synchronization and fault tolerance overhead (checkpoint I/O, straggler mitigation) often dominate the benchmark result more than peak FLOP/s.

:::

Training benchmarks validate whether hardware acceleration delivers promised training throughput. Accelerators and multi-chip systems all claim dramatic speedups, and training benchmarks reveal which claims hold under realistic workloads. They evaluate how hardware configurations, data loading mechanisms, and distributed training strategies perform when training production-scale models. These benchmarks are vital because training represents the largest capital expenditure in ML systems, and only rigorous time-to-accuracy measurement reveals whether that capital delivers proportional value rather than dissipating into scaling inefficiencies, memory bottlenecks, or communication overhead. The metrics themselves (time-to-accuracy, scaling efficiency, utilization, checkpoint overhead) are defined and worked at the scale of one machine with one to eight accelerators, the scale of the scaling-efficiency notebook below.

### Training benchmark motivation {#sec-benchmarking-training-benchmark-motivation-f365}

MLPerf Training\index{MLPerf Training!standardized framework} [@mattson2020mlperf; @mlperf_training_website] provides the standardized framework for this time-to-quality measurement. The longitudinal scaling curves in @fig-mlperf-training-improve track cumulative relative performance gains across nine model workloads between 2018 and 2024 against the orange Moore's Law baseline. Every workload curve outpaces cumulative transistor scaling (which reaches 6.6$\times$ by mid-2024), led by Mask R-CNN climbing to 48.8$\times$ and ResNet reaching 34$\times$ as distributed scaling and compiler optimizations compound hardware improvements [@tschand2025]. This trajectory documents improvements in the full hardware-software system beyond transistor scaling alone; the plotted results do not isolate the contribution of competitive pressure from other causes.

:::

Training benchmarks also expose inefficiencies such as slow data loading, underutilized accelerators, excessive memory overhead, and communication bottlenecks that erode scaling efficiency. Advertised hardware capability (for example, accelerator TFLOP/s) becomes a training speedup only to the extent that a benchmark verifies it under realistic conditions.

Training benchmarks serve four interconnected functions. First, they enable hardware and software optimization by providing vendor-neutral comparisons across accelerator architectures and frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch) on standardized tasks, guiding hardware selection for data centers and cloud environments. Software optimizations including mixed-precision training\index{Mixed-precision training!FP16 and FP32}[^fn-bench-mixed-precision] and memory-efficient data loading are similarly quantified. Second, they evaluate scalability: adding GPUs should reduce training time proportionally, but communication overhead, synchronization latency, and memory bottlenecks limit scaling efficiency in practice. Training benchmarks quantify these losses, revealing whether infrastructure investments deliver proportional returns. Third, they provide cost and energy accountability: with a single large-scale training run consuming energy on the scale of the GPT-3 estimate in @sec-benchmarking-energy-efficiency-cost-15ca, benchmarks that track cost per training run and power consumption per unit of progress help organizations balance computational power with sustainability goals. Finally, standardized evaluation criteria, controlled randomness, submission rules, and audits make comparisons more reproducible and constrain implementation-specific shortcuts.

[^fn-bench-mixed-precision]: **Mixed-precision training**\index{Mixed-precision training!benchmarking comparability}: Uses lower precision for most arithmetic while preserving higher-precision accumulation where needed [@micikevicius2017mixed]. The benchmarking consequence: mixed-precision and full-precision runs are not directly comparable because reduced memory traffic and larger feasible batch sizes can change convergence dynamics. MLPerf addresses this by fixing the accuracy target, making time-to-accuracy the comparable quantity regardless of precision strategy.

### Training metrics {#sec-benchmarking-training-metrics-0f1a}

From a systems perspective, training benchmarks assess the rate of convergence toward a verified quality threshold rather than the raw processing speed of an execution loop. Metrics such as sample throughput and scaling efficiency become meaningful only when the workload reaches target convergence; without that operational constraint, raw throughput rewards numerical instability and divergence. MLPerf Training formalizes this requirement by coupling wall-clock time directly to task-specific validation targets across each standardized workload.

#### Time and throughput {#sec-benchmarking-time-throughput-1252}

A training cluster that processes twice as many images per second by doubling the minibatch or dropping precision has not sped up training if the run requires twice as many epochs to converge—or never reaches the quality floor at all. That is why the primary metric for evaluating training efficiency is the time required to reach a predefined accuracy threshold\index{Time-to-accuracy!training benchmark primary metric}. Training time $(\TrainingTime)$ measures how long a model takes to converge to an acceptable performance level, reflecting the overall computational efficiency of the system. Let $\text{Accuracy}_{\text{val}}(\TimeInstant)$ be the model's validation accuracy at training time $\TimeInstant$, and let the target accuracy be the benchmark-specific threshold (for example, 75.9 percent top-1 accuracy for ResNet-50 on ImageNet in MLPerf). @Eq-training-time-benchmark formally defines this metric, keeping the benchmark focused on how quickly a system achieves meaningful results:
$$\TrainingTime= \inf \big\{\TimeInstant\geq 0 : \text{Accuracy}_{\text{val}}(\TimeInstant) \geq \text{target accuracy} \big\}$$ {#eq-training-time-benchmark}

A run that never reaches the target has no finite time-to-accuracy, preventing raw training speed from rewarding a system that fails the benchmark's quality criterion.

Throughput\index{Throughput!definition},[^fn-throughput-etymology-capacity] often expressed as the number of training samples processed per second, provides an additional measure of system performance. Let $\ProcessedSampleCount$ be the total number of training samples processed and $\TrainingTime$ the training time from @eq-training-time-benchmark. @Eq-throughput-benchmark makes the rate explicit by dividing processed samples by training time:
$$\text{Throughput} = \frac{\ProcessedSampleCount}{\TrainingTime}$$ {#eq-throughput-benchmark}

[^fn-throughput-etymology-capacity]: **Throughput**\index{Throughput!etymology}: Originating in manufacturing to measure units produced per unit time, the term entered computing in the 1960s batch-processing era. The manufacturing origin carries a systems lesson: throughput and latency are inherently opposed, because batching increases throughput (more units per hour) at the cost of individual item wait time. In ML serving, this manifests as the batch-size trade-off: larger batches improve GPU utilization but increase per-request latency.

Throughput alone cannot certify system capability. A platform may sustain high sample rates using aggressive low-precision formats or enormous minibatches, yet fail to reach target accuracy because of gradient divergence or poor generalization. In MLPerf Training, for instance, a ResNet-50 benchmark on ImageNet is valid only if the model achieves the required 75.9 percent top-1 validation accuracy [@mattson2020mlperf; @mlperf_training_website]. Evaluating throughput strictly as the rate of progress toward convergence ensures that reported gains reflect genuine learning productivity rather than wasted arithmetic cycles.

#### Scalability and parallelism {#sec-benchmarking-scalability-parallelism-1124}

Scalability\index{Scalability!distributed training metric} measures how effectively training performance improves as resources are added. Ideally, doubling GPU count should halve training time. In practice, communication overhead, memory bandwidth limits, and parallelization inefficiencies constrain scaling well below linear.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: scaling-efficiency-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SCALING EFFICIENCY CALCULATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Callout "Scaling Efficiency Calculation"—worked example showing
# │          strong scaling efficiency for multi-GPU ResNet-50 training
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate the practical impact of scaling efficiency.
# │ Show: That an 8-GPU cluster can lose 25 percent of its potential to overhead.
# │ How: Calculate the efficiency ratio between single-GPU and multi-GPU training times.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check, MarkdownStr

class ScalingEfficiencyCalc:
    """Strong scaling efficiency for an illustrative 8-GPU image-classifier run: 75% efficiency, 25% overhead loss."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    t1_hours = 24  # scenario input: single-GPU training time for the illustrative run
    n_gpus = 8
    tn_hours = 4  # actual N-GPU training time
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    ideal_hours = t1_hours / n_gpus
    efficiency_pct = t1_hours / (n_gpus * tn_hours) * 100
    loss_pct = 100 - efficiency_pct
    eff_denom = n_gpus * tn_hours
    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(efficiency_pct == 75.0, f"Expected 75% scaling efficiency, got {efficiency_pct:.1f}%")
    check(ideal_hours < tn_hours, "Actual multi-GPU time should be slower than perfect scaling.")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    ideal_hours_str = fmt_time(ideal_hours, "hour", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    eff_str = fmt_percent(round(efficiency_pct) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    loss_str = fmt_percent(round(loss_pct) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    eff_denom_str = fmt(eff_denom, precision=0, commas=False)
    t1_hours_str = fmt_time(t1_hours, "hour", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    t1_raw_str = fmt(t1_hours, precision=0, commas=False)
    n_gpus_str = fmt_count(n_gpus, commas=False, label="GPU")
    tn_hours_str = fmt_time(tn_hours, "hour", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    scaling_eq_str = fmt_math(
        f"\\text{{Eff}}_{{\\text{{scaling}}}}({n_gpus}) = "
        f"\\frac{{{t1_hours}\\,\\text{{hours}}}}{{{n_gpus} \\times {tn_hours}\\,\\text{{hours}}}} "
        "\\times 100\\%"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-benchmarking-scaling-efficiency-calculation .callout-notebook title="Scaling efficiency calculation"}

**Problem**: A team trains an image classifier on a fixed dataset. Single-GPU training takes `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.t1_hours_str`. With `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.n_gpus_str`, training takes `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.tn_hours_str`. Is this good scaling? Where did the efficiency go?

**Step 1**: Define scaling efficiency.
For strong scaling\index{Strong scaling!definition} (fixed problem size, more processors), let $\Time(1)$ be the training time on a single GPU, and $\Time(\AcceleratorCount)$ the training time on $\AcceleratorCount$ GPUs. @Eq-scaling-efficiency defines efficiency:
$$\text{Eff}_{\text{scaling}}(\AcceleratorCount) = \frac{\Time(1)}{\AcceleratorCount \times \Time(\AcceleratorCount)} \times 100\%$$ {#eq-scaling-efficiency}

**Step 2**: Calculate efficiency.
`{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.scaling_eq_str` = `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.t1_raw_str`/`{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.eff_denom_str` = `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.eff_str`

With perfect scaling, `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.n_gpus_str` would complete in `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.ideal_hours_str` (`{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.t1_hours_str`/`{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.n_gpus_str`). The actual `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.tn_hours_str` represents `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.eff_str` efficiency.

**Step 3**: Investigate the efficiency loss. The two elapsed times establish the "missing" `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.loss_str`, but do not attribute it. @Tbl-benchmarking-scaling-efficiency-loss lists illustrative contributions and profiling signals for gradient synchronization, memory copy, load imbalance, and batch-size effects. Strong-scaling comparisons hold total work fixed; time-to-quality comparisons must also account for any change in steps to convergence.

In multi-accelerator data-parallel training (such as 2, 4, or 8 GPUs connected over PCIe or NVLink within a host), each accelerator computes gradients on its own local slice of the minibatch. The AllReduce\index{AllReduce!gradient synchronization} collective of @sec-model-training-data-parallelism-ad1c must sum these gradients so every worker receives the identical global gradient average before the next step. Gradient tensors have one entry per trained parameter, but their byte payload equals weight storage only when their representations match. Moving them across interconnects adds communication whose cost depends on topology, the collective algorithm, and overlap. With fixed total work and ideal partitioning, compute time per step shrinks ($\IronLawComputeTime \propto 1/\AcceleratorCount$), while communication may shrink more slowly or grow. Exposed synchronization then occupies a larger fraction of the step; traces determine how much of the observed scaling loss it explains.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}
```

| **Source**                                | **Example Contribution** | **Measurement**                     |
|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------:|:------------------------------------|
| **Gradient synchronization**              |          10–15%          | AllReduce time per step             |
| **Memory copy (CPU$\leftrightarrow$GPU)** |           3–5%           | Data transfer profiling             |
| **Load imbalance**                        |           2–5%           | Per-GPU step time variance          |
| **Batch size effects**                    |           2–5%           | Larger batches converge differently |

: **Scaling Efficiency Loss Sources**: Illustrative decomposition of the missing efficiency budget into measurable overhead categories and the corresponding measurement signal used to attribute each loss. Actual percentages depend on model, interconnect, storage, batch schedule, and framework implementation. {#tbl-benchmarking-scaling-efficiency-loss}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

**Step 4**: The systems insight.
<!-- lego-ok-block: typical strong-scaling efficiency ranges at different GPU counts -->
Scaling efficiency can decrease as $\AcceleratorCount$ grows when exposed communication and other overheads fail to shrink with per-GPU compute. In this worked example, eight GPUs reach 75 percent efficiency; at larger scales, the same arithmetic makes clear why sophisticated communication and input-pipeline optimization become necessary.

MLPerf reports raw performance, while scaling efficiency can be calculated across matched submissions: a system achieving 2$\times$ throughput at 50 percent efficiency may be worse than 1.5$\times$ throughput at 90 percent efficiency, depending on cost constraints.
<!-- end lego-ok-block -->

:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The AllReduce collective that averages gradients across data-parallel workers is established in @sec-model-training-data-parallelism-ad1c.
:::

Parallelism strategies (data, model, and pipeline parallelism) and the synchronization each requires are developed in @sec-model-training-data-parallelism-ad1c; within one machine of two to eight accelerators, data parallelism\index{Data Parallelism!training strategy} is the common case. A benchmark's job is narrower: to report how much of the added capacity a configuration converts into speedup without degrading convergence. That conversion is **scaling efficiency**\index{Scaling efficiency!strong scaling definition}. While strong scaling evaluates whether adding processors reduces training time on a fixed total workload, **weak scaling**\index{Weak scaling!definition} scales the problem size proportionally with processor count to keep the per-device workload constant. It measures whether the system can train larger models or ingest larger datasets within a fixed time budget without communication bottlenecks dominating.

#### Resource utilization {#sec-benchmarking-resource-utilization-336b}

Training efficiency depends on learning speed, cluster scalability, and how effectively the hardware resources are used. Compute utilization\index{Resource utilization!compute and memory} requires an explicit numerator. Model FLOPs utilization (MFU), the metric of definition \ref{dfn-training-model-flops-utilization-mfu}, compares the useful model operation rate with the matching hardware peak; activity counters instead report whether units are busy. MFU contrasts with hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU), which counts all executed operations including activation recomputation; recomputation adds executed FLOPs without adding useful model FLOPs for the same step. Comparing them separates useful model work from work expended to relieve memory capacity limits. Low utilization may indicate bottlenecks in data movement, memory access, or inefficient workload scheduling.

For instance, when training ResNet-50, decoding and augmenting thousands of JPEG images per second on the host can limit throughput even when the accelerators have compute to spare, the crossing from compute-bound to input-bound that @sec-model-training-data-pipeline-8e71 traces. If storage retrieval or preprocessing cannot keep up, the accelerators wait. Profiling resource utilization identifies the bottleneck, and optimizations such as prefetching, caching, and more parallel input processing can improve sustained performance.

Memory bandwidth is another limiting factor, as deep learning models require frequent access to large volumes of data during training. If memory bandwidth saturates, increasing compute power alone will not improve training speed. Benchmarks assess how well models use available memory, ensuring that data transfer rates between storage, main memory, and processing units do not become performance bottlenecks.

I/O performance also plays a direct role in training efficiency, particularly when working with large datasets that cannot fit entirely in memory. Benchmarks evaluate the efficiency of data loading pipelines, including preprocessing operations, caching mechanisms, and storage retrieval speeds. Systems that fail to optimize data loading can experience large slowdowns, regardless of computational power.

#### Energy efficiency and cost {#sec-benchmarking-energy-efficiency-cost-15ca}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: gpt3-training-energy-anchor
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GPT-3 TRAINING ENERGY ANCHOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Training benchmark energy-efficiency paragraph below.
# │
# │ Goal: Keep the GPT-3 training-energy estimate local to this paragraph.
# │ Show: Estimated GPT-3 training electricity consumption.
# │ How: Read the registry-backed GPT-3 training energy and format it as MWh.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_energy
from mlsysim.core.units import MWh

class Gpt3TrainingEnergyAnchor:
    """Local registry-backed GPT-3 training-energy anchor."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Registry value) ────────────────────────────────────────
    training_energy_mwh = Models.Language.GPT3.training_energy_mwh

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt3_training_energy_mwh_str = fmt_energy(
        training_energy_mwh,
        unit=MWh,
        precision=0,
        commas=True,
    )
```

Training GPT-3\index{GPT-3!training cost} was estimated to consume `{python} Gpt3TrainingEnergyAnchor.gpt3_training_energy_mwh_str` of electricity [@patterson2021carbon]. At that scale, energy efficiency metrics\index{Energy efficiency!training cost accounting} quantify the power usage of training workloads so teams can identify systems that reach target accuracy without wasted energy. Fewer iterations reduce energy only when their total energy cost is lower; a more expensive step can offset the reduced count, so suites such as MLPerf Training measure total energy over the complete run to the same quality target. The same power accounting governs inference, where precision is one potential energy lever; @sec-benchmarking-power-measurement-techniques-bcc2 works through why INT8 quantization cuts per-inference energy by attacking both memory traffic and arithmetic cost.

Cost considerations extend beyond electricity usage to include hardware expenses, cloud computing costs, and infrastructure maintenance. Training benchmarks provide insights into the cost-effectiveness of different hardware and software configurations by measuring training time in relation to resource expenditure. Organizations can use these benchmarks to balance performance and budget constraints when selecting training infrastructure.

#### Fault tolerance and robustness {#sec-benchmarking-fault-tolerance-robustness-93e8}

Training workloads often run for extended periods, sometimes spanning days or weeks, making fault tolerance\index{Fault tolerance!training checkpoint strategy} an essential consideration. A resilient system must handle unexpected failures (hardware malfunctions, network disruptions, and memory errors) without compromising accuracy convergence.

Production systems checkpoint for fault tolerance, periodically saving progress so a failure does not restart the run. On a single host, a benchmark records the save interval, the state written, and the pause each save exposes to training. Model weights and optimizer states consume storage bandwidth, and any pause extends wall-clock time to the quality target. Asynchronous saving can overlap I/O with computation, but its staging buffers and competing storage traffic remain part of the measured workload. Cluster recovery and parallel file systems extend this problem beyond the local machine; the local benchmarking lesson is to include the intended saving behavior in sustained performance measurements. MLPerf Training primarily measures time-to-quality under standardized workloads and does not benchmark failure recovery directly.

Training runs are also where reproducibility is hardest, because stochastic processes interact with hardware-specific behavior over many hours. What a training report must preserve to make its result reproducible, the full run envelope rather than the random seed alone, is collected with the other statistical controls in @sec-benchmarking-reproducibility-standardization-7ecf.

### Training performance evaluation {#sec-benchmarking-training-performance-evaluation-bdc3}

A comprehensive training benchmark considers multiple dimensions of system behavior because each dimension identifies a different way hardware investment can fail to become convergence. @Tbl-training-metrics summarizes the core categories and associated metrics commonly used to benchmark system-level training performance, providing a framework for understanding how training systems behave under different workloads and configurations.

| **Category**                            | **Key Metrics**                                                                                                              | **Example Benchmark Use**                                   |
|:----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Training Time and Throughput**        | Time-to-accuracy (seconds, minutes, hours); Throughput (samples/sec)                                                         | Comparing training speed across different GPU architectures |
| **Scalability and Parallelism**         | Scaling efficiency (percent of ideal speedup); Communication overhead (latency, bandwidth)                                   | Analyzing distributed training performance for large models |
| **Resource Utilization**                | Compute utilization (percent GPU/TPU usage); Memory bandwidth (GB/s); I/O efficiency (data loading speed)                    | Optimizing data pipelines to improve GPU utilization        |
| **Energy Efficiency and Cost**          | Energy consumption per run (MWh, kWh); Training throughput per watt (FLOP/s/W)                                               | Evaluating energy-efficient training strategies             |
| **Fault Tolerance and Robustness**      | Checkpoint overhead (time per save); Recovery success rate (percent)                                                         | Assessing failure recovery in cloud-based training systems  |
| **Reproducibility and Standardization** | Variance across runs (percent difference in accuracy, training time); Framework consistency (TensorFlow vs. PyTorch vs. JAX) | Ensuring consistency in benchmark results across hardware   |

: **Training Benchmark Dimensions**: Key categories and metrics for evaluating machine learning training systems beyond simple speed, covering resource efficiency, reproducibility, and overall performance trade-offs across different training approaches and infrastructure configurations. {#tbl-training-metrics tbl-colwidths="[18,55,27]"}

The scaling notebook supplies a concrete interpretation of @tbl-training-metrics. The measured completion times establish a speedup and a resource-efficiency cost, but they do not identify which overhead caused the difference. A procurement decision therefore uses the time-to-quality result first, then the utilization and communication measurements to decide whether additional hardware or a different execution configuration would address the limiting resource.

Across matched runs, GPU boost-clock[^fn-gpu-boost-clock] behavior and thermal state must follow the same protocol; otherwise a short fast run can be mistaken for a durable improvement. The repeated-run controls in @sec-benchmarking-statistical-methodological-issues-7aa5 determine whether the difference exceeds experimental uncertainty.

[^fn-gpu-boost-clock]: **GPU boost clock**\index{GPU boost clock!benchmark variability}: Dynamic frequency scaling raises clocks above base when thermal and power headroom permit. Short benchmark runs can capture this burst performance, while sustained training may settle to a different operating point. The benchmark must document the measured thermal state and clock policy.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Scaling extrapolation pitfall (recap of worked example).
# │ Goal: 8-GPU scaling efficiency of the illustrative run, for distant prose reuse.
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check

class ScalingEfficiencyRecap:
    t1_hours = 24
    n_gpus = 8
    tn_hours = 4
    efficiency_pct = t1_hours / (n_gpus * tn_hours) * 100

    check(efficiency_pct == 75.0, f"Expected 75% scaling efficiency, got {efficiency_pct:.1f}%")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_str = fmt_count(n_gpus, commas=False, label="GPU")
    eff_str = fmt_percent(round(efficiency_pct) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

In the worked case, `{python} ScalingEfficiencyRecap.n_gpus_str` reach `{python} ScalingEfficiencyRecap.eff_str` scaling efficiency. If the required quality target and completion deadline are met, the configuration clears the time constraint, but the remaining scaling overhead still matters for cost. If the deadline is missed, the efficiency ratio alone does not justify buying more accelerators. The next experiment must measure exposed synchronization, input stalls, and per-device work under the intended batch and checkpoint schedule before choosing an intervention. If convergence changes between configurations, compare complete time-to-quality runs rather than interpreting the difference as pure strong-scaling loss.

A training report can therefore support a configuration choice without claiming that every measured overhead has already been explained. Its acceptance gates concern learning; an efficiently trained model still needs separate evidence that it can serve requests under deployment constraints.

::: {#chk-benchmarking-measurement-and-training .callout-checkpoint title="Measuring a training claim"}

The first half of the chapter built the measurement and applied it to training. Before moving to deployment, you should be able to:

- [ ] Restate "ResNet-50 at INT8 is faster" as a benchmark by naming its input boundary, output, quality floor, and timing statistic.
- [ ] Explain why a `{python} ComponentLatencyExample.component_speedup_mult_str` model-stage speedup inside a `{python} ComponentLatencyExample.e2e_latency_ms_str` request yields only about `{python} ComponentLatencyExample.e2e_speedup_mult_str` end to end, and name the granularity that exposes it.
- [ ] Use the roofline ceiling and the measured MLPerf throughput for ResNet-50 on one accelerator to compute its utilization, and name two candidate causes of the gap.
- [ ] Explain what MLPerf's closed division holds fixed and what its open division compares instead.
- [ ] Compute strong-scaling efficiency for a run that takes `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.t1_hours_str` on one accelerator and `{python} ScalingEfficiencyCalc.tn_hours_str` on eight, and explain why the two elapsed times alone do not attribute the loss.

:::

## Inference Benchmarks {#sec-benchmarking-inference-benchmarks-2c1f}

A camera trap running MobileNetV2 on an edge board must classify each frame within a 33-millisecond deadline to keep up with a 30-frame-per-second video stream. If an unbenchmarked garbage collection pause, dynamic batching timeout, or kernel launch hiccup stretches the p99 latency well past that deadline, frames are dropped. An animal that crosses the field of view in under a second may then go unrecorded, no matter how high the board's average throughput. An autonomous vehicle's perception loop runs against the same deadline arithmetic with far higher stakes. Training benchmarks measure how quickly a system learns; inference benchmarks measure how reliably it serves under real-world operational constraints. The two regimes differ in what they tolerate: training tolerates variable iteration times as long as gradient descent converges, but inference enforces service-level objectives where every delayed prediction compromises the application.

Inference is also where the optimization chapters converge, because the accelerated hardware runs the compressed models to deliver real-time predictions. Inference benchmarks reveal whether those theoretical speedups become actual latency reductions under realistic deployment conditions. Their central quantity is end-to-end request latency $\EndToEndRequestLatency$, the full time from a request's arrival to its response, including queueing, preprocessing, model execution, and postprocessing. It is distinct from the iron law's latency term $\Latency$, which counts only the fixed overhead (orchestration, serialization, dispatch) that one execution pays regardless of how much data it moves or arithmetic it performs. Queueing delay, which grows with load, belongs to $\EndToEndRequestLatency$ but not to $\Latency$.

::: {#dfn-benchmarking-ml-inference-benchmarks .callout-definition title="ML inference benchmarks"}

***ML inference benchmarks***\index{ML inference benchmark!definition} are machine learning system benchmarks that quantify a system's ability to meet latency constraints $(\EndToEndRequestLatency)$ at specified throughput levels, measuring scenario-defined latency statistics, throughput (queries per second), and power efficiency across representative serving scenarios.

1.  **Significance**: Inference benchmarks expose the workload- and system-specific gap between unconstrained throughput and throughput while meeting a service-level objective (SLO), such as a p99 latency target. Queuing delays push tail latency above the target at high load, and only a benchmark that enforces the target at each throughput level shows it.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike training benchmarks, which measure time-to-accuracy over a fixed dataset, inference benchmarks measure per-query response time under realistic load patterns, capturing queuing effects, batching trade-offs, and cold-start overhead that determine real-world serving economics.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that average latency is a sufficient benchmark. A low mean can coexist with a long p99 tail, and at high request rates the slowest 1 percent becomes a large number of affected users. The benchmark must report the statistic the service objective names.

:::

### Inference benchmark motivation {#sec-benchmarking-inference-benchmark-motivation-eee1}

Large-scale benchmark training commonly runs on dedicated data center hardware, whereas inference spans a wide range of deployment scenarios, from real-time applications like autonomous driving and conversational AI to mobile devices, IoT systems, and embedded processors. This diversity extends to hardware: while GPUs and TPUs dominate large-scale training, inference workloads often use specialized accelerators like NPUs\index{NPU!inference benchmarking considerations}, field-programmable gate arrays, and dedicated inference chips such as Google's Edge TPU.[^fn-edge-tpu-benchmark] Inference benchmarks evaluate how well hardware selection, model optimization, and data pipeline design work together across these deployment environments.

[^fn-edge-tpu-benchmark]: **Edge TPU (tensor processing unit)**\index{Edge TPU!operator coverage}: Google's fixed-function edge AI accelerator. It illustrates a benchmarking constraint specific to fixed-function accelerators: its headline throughput applies only to quantized TensorFlow Lite models with supported operator types, so models requiring unsupported operators fall back to the host CPU or need graph rewrites before the accelerator result is meaningful.

Deployment differences of this breadth motivate inference benchmarks, which evaluate the bottlenecks that emerge when models transition from development to production serving. The motivating factors parallel those for training (hardware optimization, scalability, cost, fair comparison) but differ in specifics. Software optimization frameworks\index{Inference!compiler, graph optimization framework} apply inference-specific techniques such as kernel fusion, precision calibration, and kernel tuning, whose impact on latency, throughput, and power efficiency must be measured under realistic conditions to confirm they deliver real improvements without degrading accuracy. Auto-tuning compilers\index{Inference!compiler auto-tuning} add a hidden variable. The compiler itself can require hours of optimization per model-hardware pair, so benchmark results reflect the tuning budget as much as the hardware capability. Comparing results across submissions requires normalizing for compiler optimization time.

Scalability concerns also shift character. Training scales by adding GPUs to reduce time-to-accuracy on a fixed workload, whereas inference must scale dynamically in response to fluctuating user demand, handling traffic spikes without violating latency guarantees. Applications that load models on demand, such as serverless deployments, also expose the model's loading time, its cold start, directly to users.

The cost and energy profile of inference differs sharply from training. Training concentrates cost in discrete runs that may recur as data, objectives, or models change; inference cost accumulates continuously with production traffic. Running an inefficient model at scale can multiply cloud compute expenses, and on battery-powered devices, excessive computation directly affects usability. Benchmarks that measure cost per inference request and efficiency per watt help organizations optimize for both performance and sustainability across deployment platforms.

MLPerf Inference extends the standardized comparison principles established for training benchmarks to deployment scenarios, defining evaluation criteria for tasks such as image classification, object detection, and speech recognition across different hardware platforms. This keeps inference comparisons reproducible under deployment constraints such as latency requirements and energy efficiency [@reddi2020].

### Inference metrics {#sec-benchmarking-inference-metrics-78d4}

A camera trap must classify each frame before the next one arrives, a voice assistant must respond quickly enough that users do not perceive lag, and a recommendation engine must score enough candidates to keep pace with user scrolling. These constraints (latency and throughput) define the performance envelope within which all serving optimizations must operate. Inference metrics formalize these real-world demands into measurable quantities, and they differ from training metrics in kind rather than degree, because the optimization target shifts from convergence rate during training to latency predictability during serving. Training optimizes for throughput and time-to-accuracy; inference optimizes for latency consistency, resource efficiency, and service-level predictability, spanning cloud data centers handling millions of requests to edge devices operating under strict power constraints.

#### Latency and tail latency {#sec-benchmarking-latency-tail-latency-5cde}

An inference service that averages 10 ms per request can still time out for thousands of users every hour if queueing bursts or garbage-collection pauses push the slowest 1 percent of requests past its deadline. Latency\index{Latency!inference real-time requirement} measures the time for an inference system to process an input and produce a prediction. Because averages conceal those high-percentile delays, benchmarks also report tail latency\index{Tail latency!p99 significance}[^fn-tail-latency-percentile]—commonly the 95th percentile (p95) or 99th percentile (p99), the time within which 95 percent or 99 percent of inferences complete. Applications with hard deadlines require explicit deadline-miss or worst-case analysis beyond these percentiles. These measurements form the basis for SLOs and SLAs, which formalize performance expectations.

[^fn-tail-latency-percentile]: **Tail latency**\index{Tail latency!fan-out amplification}: A high-percentile response time, such as p95 or p99, determines production SLO or SLA compliance only when that objective or agreement specifies the percentile. @dean2013 showed that in fan-out architectures (common in recommendation systems), even 1 percent slow responses compound: a request touching 100 backend shards has about a 63 percent chance that at least one shard hits its 1 percent tail. Benchmarks reporting only mean latency hide this failure mode.

::: {#dfn-benchmarking-slo-vs-sla .callout-definition title="SLOs and SLAs"}

***SLOs and SLAs***\index{SLO!definition}\index{SLA!definition} are performance commitment specifications for production ML serving systems: a service-level objective (SLO) is a target value or range for a service-level indicator, while an SLA is a contract that specifies service objectives and the consequences of failing to meet them.

1.  **Significance**: A latency SLO bounds end-to-end request latency $\EndToEndRequestLatency$ by setting a target for a specified latency indicator, and the iron law's $\Latency$ is only the fixed-overhead part of that budget. Request queueing and transient spikes consume part of that budget.
2.  **Distinction**: An SLO has no contractual consequence by itself, while missing an SLA objective triggers the consequences specified in the agreement, which may include credits or penalties. Teams commonly set the internal SLO tighter than the external agreement to leave operational headroom, though the definition does not require it.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that meeting average latency satisfies a tail-latency SLO. SLOs can use averages, percentiles, rates, or other indicators; when the objective is defined at p99 or p99.9, an excellent mean does not establish compliance.

:::

Engineering teams optimize toward SLOs while the business commits to SLAs. A usable latency objective also fixes the request population, the offered load, and the measurement window. Otherwise, two teams can report the same percentile threshold over different traffic mixes and reach incompatible conclusions about compliance.

::: {#chk-benchmarking-metric-selection .callout-checkpoint title="Metric selection"}

The metric shapes the optimization.

Apply three rules before finalizing metric selection:

- [ ] Throughput vs. latency: Name the objective to optimize and the quality, latency, and cost limits the benchmark must preserve.
- [ ] Tail latency: State what p99 exposes that mean latency hides.
- [ ] End-to-end: List the preprocessing, model execution, and postprocessing stages included in the reported latency.

:::

At production scale, small p99 degradations affect many users. If 1 percent of requests take 10$\times$ longer (for example, 1000 ms instead of 100 ms), 10,000 requests per million are slow enough to risk timeouts and customer churn. Search engines and recommendation systems demonstrate this sensitivity: Google's search-latency experiments found measurable reductions in daily searches per user after 100--400 ms server-side delays [@brutlag2009speed], which is why interactive services often treat sub-100 ms response times as a practical design target. Because occasional slow responses weigh heavily on user satisfaction, such services define percentile-based objectives, and large-scale systems may track deeper tails such as p99.9.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Provisioning serving capacity so that p99 latency meets its SLO under peak load is developed in @sec-model-serving-tail-latency-5376.
:::

The challenge of meeting these tail latency targets is that the source of the tail is often architectural, not algorithmic. A garbage-collected runtime, a shared kernel driver, or a priority-inversion bug in the serving stack can inject latency spikes that no model optimization will remove.

Discord's Read States service shows the effect outside machine learning. Periodic garbage-collection pauses in its Go implementation spiked p99 latency every two minutes until a rewrite in Rust removed the pauses [@discord2020rust]. A managed runtime in a feature store or retrieval path can impose the same floor on an ML service's tail, and no model optimization removes it, which is why the complete serving stack belongs inside a production latency benchmark. @Sec-model-serving-tail-latency-5376 develops the mechanisms that shape the tail under load.

#### Token latency: TTFT and TPOT {#sec-benchmarking-token-latency-ttft-tpot-4e1a}

Generative models are served one token at a time, so their latency splits into two measured quantities. **Time to first token (TTFT)**\index{Time to first token!definition} is the interval from a request's arrival to its first output token, dominated by prefill, the pass that processes the whole prompt in parallel. **Time per output token (TPOT)**\index{Time per output token!definition} is the mean interval between subsequent tokens, set by autoregressive decode. The gap between any two successive tokens is the **inter-token latency (ITL)**\index{Inter-token latency!definition}\index{Inter-token latency!throughput trade-off}, so TPOT is the average of a request's ITLs, and the ITL distribution exposes the individual stalls that the average hides. A benchmark that reports a single aggregate throughput hides both. A model can achieve high throughput in tokens per second while still feeling sluggish if the first token arrives late. It can also minimize TTFT\index{Latency!first-token, LLM responsiveness} while generating subsequent text too slowly for interactive reading.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: llm-throughput-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LLM THROUGHPUT CALCULATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Prose bullet on "tokens/s" in the LLM benchmarking
# │          metrics discussion
# │
# │ Goal: Convert abstract token rates into tangible wall-clock times.
# │ Show: That a 4× throughput gain reduces response time from 30s to 7.5s.
# │ How: Calculate response duration for a 750-token payload across token rates.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check, fmt_rate

class LLMThroughputCalc:
    """25 vs 100 tok/s on a 750-token response: 30 s vs 7.5 s—a 4× user-perceived difference."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    response_tokens = 750  # ~500 words
    slow_tokens_per_s = 25
    fast_tokens_per_s = 100
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    slow_sec = response_tokens / slow_tokens_per_s
    fast_sec = response_tokens / fast_tokens_per_s

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(slow_sec == 30.0, f"Slow throughput should yield 30.0s, got {slow_sec}")
    check(fast_sec == 7.5, f"Fast throughput should yield 7.5s, got {fast_sec}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    slow_s_str = fmt_time(slow_sec, "second", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    fast_s_str = fmt_time(fast_sec, "second", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    response_tokens_str = fmt_count(response_tokens, commas=False, label="token")
    slow_tokens_per_s_str = fmt_rate(slow_tokens_per_s, 'tokens/s', precision=0, commas=False)
    fast_tokens_per_s_str = fmt_rate(fast_tokens_per_s, 'tokens/s', precision=0, commas=False)
```

Token throughput\index{Token throughput!generation rate} translates these generation rates into user-perceived wall-clock time: for a response of `{python} LLMThroughputCalc.response_tokens_str`, a generation rate of `{python} LLMThroughputCalc.slow_tokens_per_s_str` requires `{python} LLMThroughputCalc.slow_s_str`, whereas `{python} LLMThroughputCalc.fast_tokens_per_s_str` finishes in `{python} LLMThroughputCalc.fast_s_str`. Time-to-first-token and inter-token latency\index{Inter-token latency!throughput trade-off} must therefore be reported together: one captures initial responsiveness, and the other captures sustained delivery speed. This latency split reflects contrasting computational regimes. Time-to-first-token is governed by prompt prefill, which processes tokens in parallel and is typically compute-bound. Inter-token latency is governed by autoregressive decoding, where low-batch execution often streams weights and accesses a growing KV cache with limited reuse. The resulting bandwidth pressure depends on model residency, context length, batch size, and the execution path. @Sec-model-serving-performance-metrics-ttft-tpot-b009 builds serving policies on these two measurements; the benchmarking requirement is that both are reported, under the same offered load, for every generative workload.

#### Throughput and resource metrics {#sec-benchmarking-throughput-resource-metrics-7c2b}

Latency is only half of the serving envelope. Throughput counts how many inference requests a system completes per second, typically expressed as queries per second\index{Queries per second!inference throughput metric} (QPS) or frames per second (FPS), and it is meaningful only together with the latency at which it was measured. Batching raises throughput by processing several inputs at once while adding wait time to each, so a throughput figure reported without its latency percentile and offered load says nothing about whether a serving deadline is met. A benchmark therefore reports **batch throughput**\index{Batch throughput!definition} and per-request latency as a pair at the same offered load. Choosing the batch size that balances them is a serving policy (@sec-model-serving-batching-tax); the benchmark's job is to measure both sides of that trade.

Speed alone is insufficient because inference optimizations can change model behavior. Reducing numerical precision can accelerate computation while cutting memory and energy, as the simplified MobileNetV2 energy estimate worked out in the power section shows (@sec-benchmarking-power-measurement-boundaries-982c), but lower-precision calculations can introduce accuracy degradation. Inference benchmarks therefore evaluate how well models perform under different numerical settings, such as FP32, FP16, and INT8.[^fn-int8-quantized-benchmark] Model compression techniques[^fn-model-compression-benchmarking] further improve efficiency, but their impact on model accuracy varies depending on the task and dataset. Benchmarks help determine whether these optimizations are viable for deployment, ensuring that improvements in efficiency do not come at the cost of unacceptable accuracy loss.

Beyond speed and accuracy, @tbl-inference-metrics lists the resource terms an inference benchmark must also report, and each exists because a system can pass the latency test and still fail to deploy. Memory footprint decides whether the model fits the device's budget at all, since inference rarely spans accelerators the way training can. Cold-start performance\index{Cold start latency!serverless AI impact}, the load time plus first-request latency,[^fn-cold-start-latency] exposes initialization cost to the requesting user. It dominates in serverless AI environments[^fn-serverless-ai-inference] and on devices that evict models to free memory. When provisioning, model transfer, runtime initialization, and the first response lie on the user request path, the benchmark must include them; a warm-instance result answers a different question. Scalability records whether added accelerators or concurrent models raise throughput or collide on memory bandwidth, and energy per inference (joules per inference, or QPS/W in the cloud) sets battery life on mobile devices and operating cost in data centers.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: cold-start-transfer-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COLD-START WEIGHT-TRANSFER LOWER BOUND
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: fn-cold-start-latency footnote in Throughput and resource
# │          metrics, immediately below.
# │
# │ Goal:    Compute the physical lower bound on cold-start latency for a
# │          7-billion-parameter FP16 model over PCIe 4.0.
# │ Show:    Parameter count, model size in GB, PCIe effective bandwidth, and
# │          weight-transfer time in milliseconds.
# │ How:     Model size equals params times bytes per param; transfer time
# │          equals model size divided by effective PCIe bandwidth.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_FP16, GB, ms, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_memory, fmt_params, fmt_time

class ColdStartTransferCalc:
    """FP16 weight transfer lower bound for a 7-billion-parameter model on PCIe 4.0."""

    # LOAD
    model = Models.Language.Llama2_7B
    params = model.parameters
    model_size = model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    pcie_effective_bw = 25 * (GB / second)  # Illustrative PCIe 4.0 effective bandwidth

    # EXECUTE
    transfer = (model_size / pcie_effective_bw).to(ms)

    # GUARD
    check(round(model_size.to(GB).magnitude) == 14, f"Expected ~14 GB FP16 weights, got {model_size.to(GB).magnitude:.1f}")
    check(round(transfer.to(ms).magnitude) == 560, f"Expected ~560 ms transfer, got {transfer.to(ms).magnitude:.0f}")

    # OUTPUT
    params_b_str = fmt_params(params, scale='B', precision=0, commas=False)
    model_size_gb_str = fmt_memory(model_size, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    pcie_effective_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(pcie_effective_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    transfer_ms_str = fmt_time(transfer, ms, precision=0, commas=False)
```

[^fn-cold-start-latency]: **Cold-start latency**\index{Cold start latency!physical lower bound}: The initialization time from idle state includes storage reads, host-to-accelerator transfer, and framework setup. For a `{python} ColdStartTransferCalc.params_b_str`-parameter model in FP16 (~`{python} ColdStartTransferCalc.model_size_gb_str`) already resident in host memory, PCIe 4.0 transfer at `{python} ColdStartTransferCalc.pcie_effective_gb_per_s_str` effective bandwidth alone takes ~`{python} ColdStartTransferCalc.transfer_ms_str`; storage and initialization add to it. This lower bound makes cold-start mitigation (model caching, speculative loading) a systems design requirement.

[^fn-int8-quantized-benchmark]: **INT8 (8-bit integer)**\index{INT8!calibration dependency}: INT8 sits at the aggressive end of the precision hierarchy (FP32 baseline, FP16 halves raw weight storage, INT8 quarters it), and each step demands increasing care to preserve accuracy. Post-training INT8 quantization normally fits its value ranges on a representative calibration dataset (quantization-range calibration, distinct from the confidence calibration of @sec-benchmarking-calibration-confidence-scores-matter-3669); accuracy depends on the model, operator coverage, quantization method, and how well the calibration data represent deployment inputs. INT8 benchmarks must specify whether they use post-training quantization or quantization-aware training and document any range-calibration procedure.

[^fn-model-compression-benchmarking]: **Model compression benchmarking**\index{Model compression!multi-dimensional benchmarking}: Compression impact must be measured across four dimensions simultaneously: accuracy degradation, inference speedup, memory reduction, and energy savings. A technique achieving 10$\times$ size reduction with 1 percent accuracy loss may still be unsuitable if latency misses the deployment target; unstructured pruning, for example, leaves dense execution unchanged unless a compatible sparse representation and kernel exploit the zeros.

[^fn-serverless-ai-inference]: **Serverless AI**\index{Serverless AI!cold-start benchmarking}: Deployment paradigm where models scale from zero instances on demand. Cold-start time varies with the model, runtime, storage path, hardware allocation, and provider. Benchmarks for intermittent workloads must report whether initialization and model loading are included, because warm-instance latency alone can understate user-perceived latency.

### MLPerf inference benchmarks {#sec-benchmarking-mlperf-inference-benchmarks-e878}

MLPerf Inference\index{MLPerf Inference!benchmark family evolution} turns that balance among latency, throughput, memory, energy, and accuracy into scored scenarios, and it matters because deployment context changes what a result means. The benchmark, developed by MLCommons\index{MLCommons!nonprofit benchmark consortium},[^fn-mlcommons-benchmark-suite] provides a standardized framework for evaluating machine learning inference performance across a range of deployment environments. MLPerf began with training benchmarks in 2018; MLPerf Inference was added later to standardize deployment-time evaluation across scenarios. The family of MLPerf inference benchmarks maps each benchmark to a deployment setting, so a score can be interpreted against the latency, throughput, memory, and power constraints the system will face.

[^fn-mlcommons-benchmark-suite]: **MLCommons**\index{MLCommons!open submission}: Launched in 2020 as a nonprofit consortium evolving from the 2018 MLPerf effort, MLCommons includes members across industry and academia [@mlcommons2026about]. Requiring published system specifications improves result comparability, but it does not prevent submitters from selecting which systems or workloads to enter. Published results reveal large performance differences between vendors on identical workloads, making MLCommons the closest the field has to SPEC-style like-for-like hardware comparison.

#### MLPerf Inference {#sec-benchmarking-mlperf-inference-4b4a}

MLPerf Inference [@reddi2020] is the baseline inference benchmark, defining standardized scenarios for deployment-time evaluation across data-center and edge settings. Submissions follow the closed and open divisions defined in @sec-benchmarking-communitydriven-standardization-5c56\index{Closed division!MLPerf submission}\index{Open division!MLPerf submission}. Its workloads span image classification, object detection, natural language processing, and recommendation, and its results are a common reference point for comparing accelerators and CPUs when the submission rules and scenario match the intended deployment. On recommendation workloads, scores on DLRM\index{DLRM!recommendation model benchmark}[^fn-dlrm-benchmark-recommendation] can inform choices between accelerator generations, although the size of the gain depends on workload, software stack, and system configuration. At the same time, the cost of comprehensive benchmarking limits who can participate and how thoroughly systems are evaluated.

[^fn-dlrm-benchmark-recommendation]: **DLRM (deep learning recommendation model)**\index{DLRM!capacity-bound benchmark}: Facebook's 2019 recommendation architecture combines embedding tables for categorical features with multilayer perceptrons for continuous features [@naumov2019deep]. DLRM stresses benchmarks differently than vision or language models: its embedding tables can be large enough that memory capacity and bandwidth dominate compute throughput. That makes DLRM the book's capacity-bound workload in MLPerf-style inference evaluation, revealing hardware limitations invisible to compute-bound benchmarks [@reddi2020].

::: {#psp-benchmarking-cost-comprehensive-benchmarking .callout-perspective title="The cost of comprehensive benchmarking"}

Submitting to MLPerf can require dedicated engineering effort, hardware access, tuning, validation, and careful documentation across the relevant configurations. The cost depends heavily on workload and scope, but it is high enough that submissions are dominated by major technology companies and hardware vendors, while smaller organizations rely on published results rather than conducting their own comprehensive evaluations. That barrier motivates the need for more lightweight, internal benchmarking practices that organizations can use to make informed decisions without the expense of full-scale standardized benchmarking.

:::

The rest of the MLPerf inference family narrows that baseline by deployment context. MLPerf Mobile\index{MLPerf Mobile!on-device inference} [@mlperf_mobile_website] evaluates whether a model stays responsive within smartphone power and memory limits [@janapa2022mlperf]. MLPerf Client\index{MLPerf client!local generative AI workloads} [@mlperf_client_website] asks whether consumer devices can run local generative-AI workloads, which makes CPUs, discrete GPUs, and integrated NPUs part of the benchmarked system. MLPerf Tiny\index{MLPerf Tiny!embedded AI benchmark} [@banbury2021mlperftiny] covers embedded and ultra-low-power systems, such as IoT\index{IoT!power-constrained environments} devices, wearables, and microcontrollers. Each variant keeps the same benchmark discipline while changing the binding resource.

### Mobile and edge benchmarks {#sec-benchmarking-mobile-edge-benchmarks-fd4f}

Unlike data centers with kilowatt-scale power delivery and active cooling infrastructure, mobile and edge deployments\index{Edge deployment!constraint triangle} operate within strict milliwatt- to watt-scale power envelopes and passive thermal dissipation limits. Benchmarking these systems means reporting power consumption, inference latency, and model accuracy together, because gains in one usually come at the expense of another. @Tbl-edge-vs-cloud-constraints contrasts these operational constraints against cloud environments.

```{=latex}
\begingroup
%\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
```

| **Constraint** | **Cloud Impact**     | **Edge Impact**             |
|:---------------|:---------------------|:----------------------------|
| **Power**      | Operational cost     | Device energy budget        |
| **Latency**    | Service-level target | Local response deadline     |
| **Accuracy**   | Task-quality target  | Balanced with power/latency |

: **Edge vs. Cloud Deployment Constraints**: Typical cloud deployments treat power as an operating cost and latency as a service target, while edge deployments often face tighter energy and response-time limits that constrain achievable accuracy. {#tbl-edge-vs-cloud-constraints}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

Consider a smartphone camera executing real-time object detection at 30 frames per second within a 3 W to 5 W thermal envelope. In this setting, an efficient architecture such as MobileNet serves as a realistic benchmark target where a larger ResNet model would violate thermal limits, despite the larger model's superior accuracy in cloud evaluations. An edge benchmark must therefore evaluate accuracy jointly with sustained power and thermal dissipation. The peak-versus-sustained gap (@sec-benchmarking-machine-learning-benchmarking-framework-70b8) is especially acute at the edge, because a passively cooled device sheds heat poorly. As junction temperatures rise, the dynamic thermal management (DTM) controller scales down operating voltage and clock frequency, causing sustained throughput to drop sharply below burst-mode peaks. That thermal mechanism makes the cooling configuration part of the benchmark specification.

::: {#exmp-benchmarking-benchmarking-edge .callout-example title="Benchmarking the edge"}

**Scenario**: An edge engineering team benchmarks a candidate chip for the camera trap's board with a vendor-advertised "1 W AI" power specification.

**Diagnosis**: Early burst-mode testing matches vendor claims, but continuous inference loop execution builds up junction heat, triggering thermal throttling and dropping steady-state throughput.

**Systems lesson**: Short burst benchmarks obscure long-term thermal throttling. Benchmarking edge ML workloads requires continuous, sustained execution testing to reflect true operational hardware limits.

:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol1_benchmarking_margin_003.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="FPS holds briefly then drops at thermal throttling knee."}

*Burst benchmark FPS collapses once thermal throttling sets in.*
:::

Throttling is the most visible way a short measurement flatters edge hardware. Idle power, duty cycle, and the data movement around the accelerator can distort a headline number too, so each needs checking before a vendor claim informs a design decision.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Edge benchmark reality-check callout (peak-vs-sustained).
# │ Goal: Keep a vendor-peak vs. sustained-throughput scenario local to the callout.
# └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Hardware
from mlsysim.core.units import TOPS, milliwatt, second, watt
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_ops_rate, fmt_percent, fmt_power, fmt_qty_range, fmt_time

class MobileNpuScenario:
    """Illustrative mobile NPU peak-throughput scenario for the sustained-performance contrast."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    peak = 45 * TOPS  # scenario assumption: advertised mobile NPU marketing peak
    sustained = 20 * TOPS  # scenario assumption: sustained thermal-throttled NPU throughput
    min_sustained_duration = 30 * second  # scenario assumption: minimum sustained benchmark window
    idle_power = 50 * milliwatt  # scenario assumption: idle device draw
    active_power = 2 * watt  # scenario assumption: active inference draw
    duty_cycle = 0.01  # scenario assumption: inference active share
    tdp_low = 3 * watt  # scenario assumption: mobile edge thermal envelope lower bound
    tdp_high = 5 * watt  # scenario assumption: mobile edge thermal envelope upper bound

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    effective_power = idle_power * (1 - duty_cycle) + active_power * duty_cycle

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(44 <= peak.to(TOPS).magnitude <= 46, "Illustrative peak should be ~45 TOPS.")
    check(sustained < peak, "Sustained throughput should be below advertised peak.")
    check(idle_power < effective_power < active_power, "Duty-cycle power should sit between idle and active power.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    mobile_peak_tops_str = fmt_ops_rate(peak, unit=TOPS, precision=0, commas=False)
    mobile_sustained_tops_str = fmt_ops_rate(sustained, unit=TOPS, precision=0, commas=False)
    min_sustained_duration_str = fmt_time(min_sustained_duration, second, precision=0, commas=False)
    idle_power_mw_str = fmt_power(idle_power, unit=milliwatt, precision=0, commas=False)
```
